questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: The graph shown below is the titration curve of a biochemical compound. Which of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B

options.label: B
options.text: The points A and B represent the range of maximum ionization of the amine and carboxyl group

options.label: C
options.text: The compound has three ionisable side chains

options.label: D
options.text: The compound has one ionisable group

questions.answerText: The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B

 

The graph is a titration curve that shows the relationship between the pH of a solution and the amount of NaOH added. Points A and B correspond to regions where the pH does not change significantly despite the addition of NaOH, indicating buffering zones. These regions represent the maximum buffering capacity of the compound, which occurs when the pH is near the pKa values of the ionizable groups in the compound.

 

At points A and B, the compound resists changes in pH, which corresponds to the ionizable groups being in equilibrium between protonated and deprotonated forms. This buffering capacity is critical because it stabilizes the pH of the solution in that range.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. The points A and B represent the range of maximum ionization of the amine and carboxyl group: This statement is incorrect. While A and B represent buffering regions, they do not specifically correspond to the ionization of amine and carboxyl groups. The pKa values for those groups depend on the specific compound in question, and the titration curve alone does not specify these groups.

 

Option C. The compound has three ionizable side chains: The titration curve has two distinct buffering regions, corresponding to two ionizable groups, not three.

 

Option D. The compound has one ionizable group: The presence of two distinct buffering regions (A and B) suggests that the compound has two ionizable groups, not one.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The titration curve shows two ionizable groups, and the maximum buffering capacity occurs at points A and B, where the pH remains relatively constant despite the addition of NaOH.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following are products of triacylglycerol breakdown and subsequent β-oxidation that may undergo gluconeogenesis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Propionyl-CoA

 

During the breakdown of triacylglycerols, fatty acids undergo β-oxidation to produce energy. However, most products of fatty acid breakdown, such as acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies, cannot undergo gluconeogenesis because they do not provide the necessary carbon skeleton to synthesize glucose.

 

The exception is propionyl-CoA, which is a product of the β-oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids. Propionyl-CoA is converted to succinyl-CoA, which is an intermediate in the Krebs cycle and can enter the gluconeogenesis pathway to produce glucose. Thus, propionyl-CoA is the only product of triacylglycerol breakdown and β-oxidation that can contribute to gluconeogenesis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Acetyl-CoA: Acetyl-CoA cannot be used directly for gluconeogenesis because it cannot be converted back to pyruvate or enter the gluconeogenesis pathway. Instead, it enters the Krebs cycle or is used for ketone body production.

 

Option C. All ketone bodies: Ketone bodies are not substrates for gluconeogenesis; they are used for energy during fasting states but cannot be converted into glucose.

 

Option D. Some amino acids: While some amino acids (glucogenic amino acids) can undergo gluconeogenesis, they are not products of triacylglycerol breakdown or β-oxidation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Propionyl-CoA, produced from the β-oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids, is the only product from triacylglycerol breakdown that can undergo gluconeogenesis. Acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies cannot be converted to glucose.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A certain class of disease is produced because of the tissue’s lack of certain metabolic pathways. Which one of the following tissues can metabolize glucose, fatty acids, and ketone bodies for ATP production?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Muscle

 

Muscle is the only tissue that can utilize glucose, fatty acids, and ketone bodies for ATP production, depending on the availability of substrates and the metabolic state of the body.

Glucose is used during normal conditions and after meals.

 

Fatty acids are used during fasting or prolonged exercise when glucose stores are depleted.

 

Ketone bodies are used during prolonged fasting or starvation, as the liver produces them when glucose levels are low.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Liver and C. Hepatocytes:  While the liver metabolizes glucose and fatty acids, it cannot utilize ketone bodies for energy, because they lack the enzyme thiophorase required for ketone body utilization.


Option D. Brain: The brain can use glucose and ketone bodies, but it cannot utilize fatty acids for energy, because they cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Muscle is the tissue that can metabolize glucose, fatty acids, and ketone bodies for ATP production, making it versatile in energy utilization under different physiological conditions.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Which reaction in the diagram below would be inhibited in the presence of large amounts of avidin, an egg white protein that binds and sequesters biotin?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C

 

Avidin, found in raw egg whites, binds to and sequesters biotin, leading to biotin deficiency. Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylase enzymes, which play a key role in various metabolic processes.

 

In the diagram, reaction C represents the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate. This reaction is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase, which requires biotin as a cofactor. When avidin binds biotin, it prevents biotin from functioning as a cofactor, inhibiting the action of pyruvate carboxylase. As a result, the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate (reaction C) would be inhibited.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. D: Reaction D involves the conversion of pyruvate to alanine, and Reaction E involves the conversion of pyruvate to lactate, neither of which require biotin.

 

Option C. B: Reaction B is the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA, catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase, which requires thiamine (vitamin B1) as a cofactor, not biotin.

 

Option D. A: Reaction A involves the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, catalyzed by pyruvate kinase. This reaction does not require biotin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of avidin, which binds and sequesters biotin, inhibits the biotin-dependent enzyme pyruvate carboxylase, blocking the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, as represented by reaction C in the diagram.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding liver enzyme dephosphorylation to phosphorylation?

options.label: C
options.text: More commonly seen in fed state than in fasting state

options.label: D
options.text: Always activated by cAMP dependent tyrosine kinase

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Catecholamines stimulate it

 

Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation are mechanisms that regulate enzyme activity. Some enzymes are activated by phosphorylation, while others are inactivated. In the liver, the regulation of these enzymes depends on the hormonal state (fed or fasting) and is mediated by signaling pathways.

 

Catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine), along with glucagon, stimulate the cAMP pathway, which activates protein kinase A (PKA). This leads to the phosphorylation of specific enzymes, such as glycogen phosphorylase, which is activated by phosphorylation to increase glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis), and glycogen synthase, which is inactivated by phosphorylation to prevent glycogen synthesis. Thus, catecholamines stimulate phosphorylation of enzymes in the liver during fasting to mobilize glucose, which confirms option B.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Always activates the enzyme: Phosphorylation does not always activate enzymes. Some enzymes, like glycogen phosphorylase, are activated by phosphorylation, while others, like glycogen synthase, are inactivated. Therefore, option A is incorrect.

 

Option C. More commonly seen in fed state than in fasting state: Phosphorylation is more commonly seen in the fasting state. During fasting, glucagon and catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) are elevated, leading to phosphorylation of key enzymes to promote glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis. In the fed state, insulin predominates, leading to dephosphorylation of enzymes, activating pathways like glycogen synthesis. Hence, option C is incorrect because phosphorylation is seen in the fasting state, not the fed state.

 

Option D. Always activated by cAMP dependent tyrosine kinase: cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), not tyrosine kinase. The cAMP pathway activates PKA, which then phosphorylates enzymes. Tyrosine kinases are part of other signaling pathways, not directly involved in cAMP-dependent regulation of liver enzymes. Thus, option D is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Phosphorylation of liver enzymes is stimulated by catecholamines and is typically seen in the fasting state, when hormones like glucagon and epinephrine activate the cAMP-PKA pathway, leading to enzyme regulation for metabolic control.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: In this transamination reaction (shown in the diagram), which of the following are the products X and Y:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Aspartate, α-ketoglutarate

 

This diagram represents a transamination reaction, a process in which an amino group is transferred from one amino acid to a keto acid, resulting in the formation of a new amino acid and a new keto acid.

 

Glutamate is a 5-carbon amino acid that can transfer its amino group to oxaloacetate (a 4-carbon keto acid), converting oxaloacetate into aspartate, which is also a 4-carbon amino acid.

 

In this process, glutamate is converted into α-ketoglutarate by losing its amino group. Oxaloacetate, upon gaining the amino group, is converted into aspartate.

 

Thus, X (the product formed from oxaloacetate) is aspartate, and Y (the product formed from glutamate) is α-ketoglutarate.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alanine, α-ketoglutarate: This is incorrect because oxaloacetate is transaminated to form aspartate, not alanine.

 

Option C. Glutamate, alanine: This is incorrect because the products are aspartate and α-ketoglutarate, not glutamate or alanine.

 

Option D. Pyruvate, aspartate: This is incorrect because glutamate is converted to α-ketoglutarate, not pyruvate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a transamination reaction, oxaloacetate is converted to aspartate, and glutamate is converted to α-ketoglutarate. This reaction is catalyzed by transaminases, and the cofactor for this process is vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate).

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: SYBR green dye is used in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Real time PCR

 

SYBR green dye is specifically used in real-time PCR. In normal PCR, DNA is amplified exponentially (1 DNA to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 8, and so on), producing many copies of the target DNA in a short amount of time. To monitor this DNA amplification as it happens, SYBR green dye is added in real-time PCR. This dye binds to double-stranded DNA and emits fluorescence when attached. As PCR progresses and the amount of double-stranded DNA increases, the fluorescence intensity also increases.

 

If SYBR green dye is free and unattached, it does not emit fluorescence. However, as the amplification proceeds (1 to 2, 2 to 4, etc.), the dye binds to the newly formed DNA, and the fluorescence increases proportionally with the amount of synthesized DNA. By measuring the intensity of the fluorescence, the amount of DNA produced can be monitored and quantified in real-time. This is why real-time PCR is also known as quantitative PCR, as it allows for the measurement of how much DNA has been synthesized by analyzing the fluorescence levels at each stage of the PCR cycle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mass spectrometry: Mass spectrometry is a technique used to measure the mass-to-charge ratio of ions. It is not involved in DNA amplification or monitoring processes like real-time PCR, and it does not utilize SYBR green dye.

 

Option C. RFLP detection: RFLP (Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism) detection is a technique for analyzing the variation in DNA sequences. It involves cutting DNA into fragments but does not use SYBR green dye or the real-time monitoring of DNA amplification.

 

Option D. FISH: FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) is a technique used to detect specific DNA sequences on chromosomes using fluorescent probes. While it involves fluorescence, it does not use SYBR green dye or perform real-time monitoring of DNA amplification as in PCR.

 

Educational Objective:


SYBR green dye is a fluorescent dye used in real-time PCR to monitor and quantify the amount of double-stranded DNA produced during the amplification process. This enables real-time monitoring, making the process also known as quantitative PCR.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following is synthesized by DNA primase during replication?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) RNA primer


DNA primase is an enzyme responsible for synthesizing the RNA primer during DNA replication. The RNA primer is a short sequence of RNA nucleotides that provides a starting point for DNA polymerase to begin synthesizing the new DNA strand. DNA polymerase cannot initiate the synthesis of DNA on its own; it requires an existing strand, which is provided by the RNA primer.

 

During replication, primase lays down RNA primers on both the leading and lagging strands. On the lagging strand, multiple RNA primers are synthesized, each initiating the formation of an Okazaki fragment. These RNA primers are later removed and replaced with DNA by DNA polymerase I.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. DNA primer: DNA primase does not synthesize DNA primers. It only synthesizes RNA primers during DNA replication. DNA polymerase uses these RNA primers to start DNA synthesis.

 

Option C. Okazaki fragments: Okazaki fragments are short DNA fragments synthesized on the lagging strand during replication. Although primase synthesizes the RNA primer that initiates each Okazaki fragment, primase itself does not produce the DNA of the Okazaki fragments.

 

Option D. Leading strand: The leading strand is the continuous DNA strand synthesized in the 5' to 3' direction during DNA replication. While an RNA primer is required to start the synthesis of the leading strand, the leading strand itself is synthesized by DNA polymerase, not DNA primase.

 

Educational Objective:


DNA primase synthesizes the RNA primer, which is essential for initiating DNA synthesis during replication.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Wobble hypothesis explains which of the following concepts of the genetic code?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Degeneracy


The Wobble hypothesis explains the concept of degeneracy in the genetic code. Degeneracy refers to the fact that more than one codon can code for the same amino acid. According to the Wobble hypothesis, the third nucleotide in a codon is less specific, meaning that different codons with variations in the third position can still code for the same amino acid. For example, serine is coded by multiple codons, and this flexibility in the third nucleotide position allows for minor variations without altering the amino acid that is incorporated into the protein.

 

In other words, while the first two nucleotides of a codon are highly specific, the third nucleotide can "wobble," allowing for several different codons to specify the same amino acid. This explains why amino acids can be coded by more than one codon, a key feature of the degeneracy of the genetic code.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Universal: The genetic code is largely universal, meaning it is shared by almost all living organisms. However, this is not explained by the Wobble hypothesis, which deals with the flexibility in codon recognition rather than the universality of the code.

 

Option B. Unambiguous: The genetic code is unambiguous, meaning each codon specifies only one amino acid. However, this does not relate to the Wobble hypothesis, which addresses how multiple codons can code for the same amino acid, not how a specific codon corresponds to a specific amino acid.

 

Option D. Non-punctuated: The genetic code is non-punctuated, meaning that codons are read sequentially without gaps or punctuation between them. This feature of the genetic code is not related to the Wobble hypothesis, which deals specifically with the flexibility of codon-anticodon pairing.

 

Educational Objective:


The Wobble hypothesis explains the degeneracy of the genetic code by allowing flexibility in the third position of a codon, enabling multiple codons to code for the same amino acid.

questions.stem: If glycogen is used for anaerobic glycolysis in muscle, there is net gain of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 3 ATP


When glycogen undergoes anaerobic glycolysis in muscle, glycogen is broken down to glucose-1-phosphate by glycogen phosphorylase, then converted to glucose-6-phosphate. No ATP is used in this process. Glucose-6-phosphate enters glycolysis, where it is converted into two molecules of lactate.

 

During this conversion, 1 ATP are used, and 4 ATP are produced, giving a net gain of 3 ATP because the ATP-consuming step is bypassed.

 

Educational Objective:


The net gain of ATP in anaerobic glycolysis when glycogen is the substrate is 3 ATP, due to the bypassing of the ATP-consuming step in the breakdown of glycogen.

questions.stem: Assertion: Patient of aldolase B deficiency was seen in the OPD. Feeding of fructose will cause hypoglycemia in the patient.Reason: Fructose 1-phosphate inhibits liver phosphorylase.

options.label: A
options.text: A and R both correct and R is explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: A and R both correct but R is not explanation of A

questions.answerText: A and R both correct and R is explanation of A
questions.solutionHtml:
d R is explanation of A


In a patient with aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance), fructose is metabolized into fructose-1-phosphate, which accumulates in the liver. This accumulation traps phosphate, leading to inhibition of glycogen phosphorylase, which is essential for glycogen breakdown. As a result, hypoglycemia occurs after fructose ingestion. Therefore, both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason explains the assertion.

 

Educational Objective:
 

In aldolase B deficiency, fructose metabolism leads to the accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate, which inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, causing hypoglycemia.



ore, both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason explains the assertion. Educational Objective: In aldolase B deficiency, fructose metabolism leads to the accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate, which inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, causing hypoglycemia.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes are involved in gluconeogenesis? Pyruvate kinasePEP CarboxykinasePyruvate carboxylaseGlyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2, 3, 4

 

Gluconeogenesis is the metabolic process that generates glucose from non-carbohydrate sources. This process requires specific enzymes that bypass the irreversible steps of glycolysis:

 

Statement 2. PEP Carboxykinase (PEPCK): Converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), facilitating the production of glucose.

 

Statement 3. Pyruvate carboxylase: Converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in the mitochondria, a necessary step in gluconeogenesis.

 

Statement 4. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase: Functions in the reversible conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, which is part of the gluconeogenesis pathway.

 

These enzymes are required to bypass glycolytic steps and push the metabolic pathway toward glucose synthesis.

 

Incorrect Statement:

 

Statement 1. Pyruvate kinase: Incorrect, as Pyruvate kinase is involved in glycolysis, not gluconeogenesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Key enzymes in gluconeogenesis include PEP Carboxykinase, Pyruvate carboxylase, and Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, while Pyruvate kinase is specific to glycolysis.

questions.stem: Production of fructose in seminal fluid is:

options.label: B
options.text: Glucose 6 PO4 → Sorbitol PO4 → fructose PO4 → fructose

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glucose 6 PO4 → glucose → Sorbitol → fructose


The production of fructose in seminal fluid occurs via the sorbitol pathway. In this process, glucose 6-phosphate is converted to glucose, which is further converted to sorbitol by aldose reductase. Finally, sorbitol is converted into fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase. This pathway is essential for the generation of fructose, which serves as an energy source for spermatozoa in seminal fluid.

 

Educational Objective:


Fructose is produced in seminal fluid through the sorbitol pathway, where glucose is first converted into sorbitol and then into fructose.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: In the figure below, which letter designates a reaction that may be catalyzed by different enzymes in different tissues, playing an important role in regulation of serum glucose levels?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Letter A


The reaction labeled A represents the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which is catalyzed by hexokinase in most tissues and by glucokinase in the liver and pancreas. These two enzymes have different regulatory properties and tissue distributions, which play a crucial role in maintaining blood glucose levels. In the liver, glucokinase has a lower affinity for glucose, allowing it to regulate glucose storage and release, particularly after meals when blood glucose levels are high. This difference in enzymatic regulation in various tissues makes reaction A important in the regulation of serum glucose levels.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Letter B: This represents phosphohexose isomerase, which is involved in the glycolytic pathway. However, it is not regulated by different enzymes in different tissues.

 

Option C. Letter C: This step involves phosphofructokinase, which is a rate-limiting enzyme for glycolysis but is not catalyzed by different enzymes in different tissues.

 

Option D. Letter D: This represents the aldolase reaction, which is also not catalyzed by different enzymes in different tissues.

 

Educational Objective:


The reaction of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate (labeled A) is catalyzed by different enzymes, hexokinase and glucokinase, in various tissues, playing an important role in the regulation of serum glucose levels.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Which reaction in the figure below occurs in both muscle and liver but has substantially different qualities in the two?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Reaction B


Reaction B, which represents the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, occurs in both muscle and liver, but the enzymes involved have different properties in the two tissues. In the liver, this reaction is catalyzed by glucokinase, while in muscle, it is catalyzed by hexokinase. These enzymes have different kinetic properties and regulatory mechanisms. Glucokinase in the liver has a higher Km (lower affinity) for glucose and is not inhibited by its product, allowing the liver to take up glucose only when blood glucose levels are high. In contrast, hexokinase in muscle has a lower Km (higher affinity) for glucose and is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, ensuring efficient glucose utilization even at low glucose concentrations.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Reaction A: This reaction occurs in the liver but not in muscle, as glucose-6-phosphatase is absent in muscle.

 

Option C. Reaction C: This reaction is part of glycolysis and occurs similarly in both liver and muscle without significant differences.

 

Option D. Reaction D: Like reaction C, this step is part of glycolysis and does not show substantial differences between muscle and liver.

 

Educational Objective:


The conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate occurs in both liver and muscle, but the enzymes involved, glucokinase and hexokinase, differ in their regulatory properties.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following is an activator of LCAT?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Apo AI


LCAT (Lecithin-Cholesterol Acyltransferase) is an enzyme that plays a critical role in the maturation of HDL by converting free cholesterol into cholesteryl ester, which is then sequestered into the core of the HDL particle. Apo AI is the main activator of LCAT, promoting this enzymatic activity, and is primarily associated with HDL particles.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apo B100: This is primarily involved in LDL metabolism and does not activate LCAT.

 

Option B. Apo B48: This is involved in chylomicron formation and transport of dietary fats but is not an activator of LCAT.

 

Option C. Apo E: This plays a role in receptor-mediated uptake of lipoproteins but is not an activator of LCAT.

 

Educational Objective:


Apo AI is the primary activator of LCAT, which is essential for the maturation of HDL particles.

questions.stem: Assertion: Acetoacetate, Beta hydroxybutyrate, and Acetone are compounds termed as ketone bodies. The liver is an organ that cannot utilize Ketone bodies. Reason: All enzymes for ketone body synthesis are present in liver mitochondria.

options.label: A
options.text: A and R both correct and R is explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: A and R both correct but R is not explanation of A

questions.answerText: A and R both correct but R is not explanation of A
questions.solutionHtml:
ion of A

 

The assertion is correct because acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone are indeed ketone bodies synthesized by the liver. However, the liver cannot utilize these ketone bodies because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase which is required for ketone body utilization. The reason is also correct, as all enzymes necessary for ketone body synthesis are present in liver mitochondria. However, this reason does not explain why the liver cannot utilize ketone bodies, making option b the correct answer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

While the liver synthesizes ketone bodies, it cannot utilize them due to the absence of thiophorase, even though all enzymes for synthesis are present in liver mitochondria.

questions.stem: In which type of hypertriglyceridemia are chylomicrons and VLDL remnants increased?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) III


Type III hyperlipoproteinemia is characterized by the accumulation of both chylomicrons and VLDL remnants. This condition, also known as familial dysbetalipoproteinemia or broad beta disease, occurs due to defects in the ApoE gene, which impairs the clearance of these remnants from the bloodstream. As a result, patients exhibit elevated levels of both chylomicrons and VLDL remnants, leading to hypertriglyceridemia.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. I: This type is characterized by elevated chylomicrons alone, without an increase in VLDL remnants.

 

Option B. IIa: This type is characterized by elevated LDL, not chylomicrons or VLDL remnants.

 

Option D. IV: This type is characterized by elevated VLDL, but not chylomicrons or their remnants.

 

Educational Objective:
 

In Type III hyperlipoproteinemia, both chylomicrons and VLDL remnants are elevated due to defective clearance, leading to hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.stemHtml: For each item listed below, select the appropriate location from the drawing shown above:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) HMG – CoA lyase – B

 

  • Carnitine shuttle - C
  • F0F1 ATP synthase – A
  • HMG – CoA lyase – B
  • Carnitine acyltransferase-1 – C


The Carnitine shuttle includes three enzymes: CPT1, CPT2, and translocase. CPT1 is located in the outer mitochondrial membrane, and CPT2 and translocase are situated in the inner mitochondrial membrane. In the image, the Carnitine shuttle corresponds to C.

 

F0F1 ATP synthase is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it plays a key role in oxidative phosphorylation, converting ADP to ATP using the proton gradient. The correct location for F0F1 ATP synthase is A.

 

HMG-CoA lyase is responsible for ketone body synthesis and is found in the mitochondrial matrix. In the diagram, the mitochondrial matrix is represented by B.

 

Carnitine acyltransferase-1 (CPT1), another name for CPT1, is located in the outer mitochondrial membrane, which is C in the diagram.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The Carnitine shuttle involves enzymes located in both the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes, with CPT1 located in the outer mitochondrial membrane. F0F1 ATP synthase is part of the inner mitochondrial membrane, while HMG-CoA lyase operates in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and fever. After a thorough examination, the attending physician decides to perform a lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis. During the procedure, as the needle is advanced, it pierces several anatomical structures before entering the lumbar cistern. Which of the following structures is pierced immediately before entering the lumbar cistern?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Arachnoid mater

 

The lumbar cistern is a cerebrospinal fluid-filled space within the subarachnoid space, located below the termination of the spinal cord at approximately L1-L2. During a lumbar puncture, a needle passes through multiple anatomical layers before entering the lumbar cistern. These layers include:

 

  1. Skin
  2. Subcutaneous tissue
  3. Supraspinous ligament
  4. Interspinous ligament
  5. Ligamentum flavum
  6. Dura mater
  7. Arachnoid mater

 

The arachnoid mater is the final structure pierced before the needle enters the lumbar cistern. This layer is part of the meninges, lying directly beneath the dura mater and just above the cerebrospinal fluid within the subarachnoid space.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ligamentum flavum: The ligamentum flavum is one of the earlier structures pierced during the lumbar puncture. It is located posterior to the dura mater and serves as a key landmark for identifying the epidural space. However, it is not the last structure pierced before entering the lumbar cistern.

 

Option C. Pia mater: The pia mater is the innermost meningeal layer that closely adheres to the surface of the spinal cord. It is not pierced during a lumbar puncture, as the procedure is designed to access the subarachnoid space without contacting the spinal cord or its associated structures.

 

Option D. Dura mater: The dura mater is the tough, outermost meningeal layer. It is pierced immediately before the arachnoid mater but is not the final structure the needle passes through before entering the lumbar cistern.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During a lumbar puncture, the arachnoid mater is the final structure pierced before the needle enters the lumbar cistern, which contains cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A patient came to the OPD with history of vision loss. On investigation optic chiasma was found compressed due to an aneurysm. Which artery is most commonly involved in such presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Anterior communicating artery

 

The optic chiasma is a critical structure where fibers from the nasal retina of both eyes cross. Compression of the optic chiasma typically results in bitemporal hemianopia, a pattern of vision loss affecting the outer halves of the visual fields. One of the most common causes of optic chiasma compression is an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery (AComA).

 

 

 

The AComA is a part of the Circle of Willis and lies in close proximity to the optic chiasma. When an aneurysm occurs in this artery, it can expand and exert pressure on the optic chiasma, leading to the characteristic vision changes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery: While the anterior cerebral artery is part of the Circle of Willis, its course does not directly bring it into close proximity with the optic chiasma. It is less likely to cause compression of the optic chiasma during an aneurysm.

 

Option B. Middle cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery supplies lateral parts of the brain and is not anatomically close to the optic chiasma. It is not typically implicated in vision loss due to compression of the optic chiasma.

 

Option C. Anterior choroidal artery: The anterior choroidal artery supplies structures such as the optic tract and lateral geniculate body but does not directly compress the optic chiasma in cases of aneurysm.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Compression of the optic chiasma, leading to bitemporal hemianopia, is most commonly caused by an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with sudden onset of violent, involuntary throwing movements of his right arm and leg. These movements are continuous and have significantly impaired his daily activities. His medical history is significant for hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Imaging studies reveal a lesion in the brain. Which of the following structures is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Subtalamic Nucleus

 

The patient's symptoms are consistent with hemiballismus, characterized by violent, involuntary, and flinging movements of one side of the body. This condition is typically caused by a lesion in the subthalamic nucleus, part of the basal ganglia.

 

 

  • The subthalamic nucleus plays a crucial role in the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia, which inhibits excessive motor activity.
  • A lesion in the subthalamic nucleus results in reduced inhibition, leading to overactive motor circuits and the characteristic violent movements seen in hemiballismus.
  • Common causes of subthalamic nucleus lesions include ischemic stroke, often related to hypertension and diabetes mellitus, as seen in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Caudate Nucleus: The caudate nucleus is part of the basal ganglia and plays a role in motor and cognitive functions. Lesions here are more often associated with conditions such as Huntington’s disease, which leads to chorea, a smoother, "dancing-like" movement, rather than the violent flinging movements seen in hemiballismus.

 

Option B. Thalamus: The thalamus acts as a relay station for sensory and motor signals. While thalamic lesions can cause motor dysfunction, they do not specifically lead to hemiballismus.

 

Option C. Substantia Nigra: The substantia nigra is involved in dopamine production and is implicated in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, which is characterized by bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor, rather than the violent movements observed in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hemiballismus is caused by a lesion in the subthalamic nucleus, resulting in violent, involuntary flinging movements on the opposite side of the body.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A patient complains of headache with periorbital pain, tearing/ lacrimation, drooling of saliva, jaw spasm/pain, with light and accommodation reflex normal and pupils neither dilated nor constricted. Features of the patient can be explained by the involvement of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C

 

The patient’s symptoms, including periorbital pain, tearing, lacrimation, jaw spasm, and drooling of saliva, are hallmark features of trigeminal neuralgia. The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is primarily involved.

 

 

The trigeminal nerve has three divisions:

 

  1. Ophthalmic (V1) - Provides sensory innervation to the periorbital region.
  2. Maxillary (V2) - Responsible for sensory innervation to the midface, including the lacrimal gland and nasal structures.
  3. Mandibular (V3) - Provides sensory innervation to the lower face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication, explaining the jaw spasm.

 

The lacrimation, tearing, and salivation are mediated through parasympathetic innervation associated with the trigeminal nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion. Jaw spasm is due to involvement of the mandibular branch (V3), which innervates the muscles of mastication.

 

The light and accommodation reflexes being normal indicate that the third cranial nerve (oculomotor) is not affected, further pointing towards the trigeminal nerve as the culprit.

 

On the provided brainstem image, C corresponds to the trigeminal nerve, the largest cranial nerve originating from the ventral pons, confirming the answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A (Olfactory Nerve): The olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) is responsible for the sense of smell. It is unrelated to the described symptoms of periorbital pain, lacrimation, or jaw spasm.

 

Option B. B (Optic Nerve): The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) is responsible for vision and is not involved in the sensory or motor functions described in this patient’s case.

 

Option D. D (Facial Nerve): While the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) plays a role in lacrimation and salivation, it does not explain the periorbital pain, conjunctival reflex involvement, or jaw spasm. These are specifically linked to the trigeminal nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Trigeminal neuralgia involves the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) and can cause periorbital pain, lacrimation, tearing, and jaw spasm due to its extensive sensory and motor functions. The nerve originates from the ventral surface of the pons, as seen in the labeled image (C).

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the clinic with difficulty in speech production. She is able to understand language but struggles to form coherent sentences. Neurological examination and imaging studies reveal a lesion affecting a specific area of the brain. Which of the following areas is most likely involved in her condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
;

The description of the brain regions in the explanation aligns with the role of the inferior frontal gyrus as the site of Broca's area.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Superior temporal gyrus: The superior temporal gyrus contains Wernicke’s area (Brodmann area 22), which is involved in language comprehension. Lesions in this region lead to Wernicke’s aphasia, characterized by fluent but nonsensical speech and impaired comprehension, not the symptoms seen in this patient.

 

Option C. Angular gyrus: The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) is involved in language processing, particularly reading and writing. Damage to this region results in symptoms such as alexia (inability to read) or agraphia (inability to write), which are not described in this case.

 

Option D. Postcentral gyrus: The postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2) is the primary somatosensory cortex and is involved in processing sensory input from the body. A lesion here would cause sensory deficits rather than language or speech production difficulties.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Difficulty in speech production with preserved comprehension is characteristic of Broca’s aphasia, caused by a lesion in Broca’s area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the structure marked in the image given below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fornix

 

The structure marked in the image is the fornix, a major white matter tract of the brain. The fornix is part of the limbic system and plays a crucial role in transmitting signals from the hippocampus to other parts of the brain, including the mammillary bodies and the thalamus.

 

 

  • Anatomical Location: The fornix is located beneath the corpus callosum, arching over the thalamus in the midline section of the brain.
  • Function: It is primarily involved in memory consolidation and connects structures important for emotion and memory.

 

The arrow in the image points to the distinct curved structure of the fornix, confirming its identity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pineal gland: The pineal gland is a small endocrine gland located between the two hemispheres of the brain in a groove where the two halves of the thalamus join. It is not the structure marked in the image, as the arrow points to the fornix.

 

Option B. Falx cerebri: The falx cerebri is a dural fold that separates the two cerebral hemispheres along the midline. It is not a white matter tract and is located above the corpus callosum, making it an incorrect option.

 

Option D. Pituitary gland: The pituitary gland is located at the base of the brain, within the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone. It is part of the endocrine system and is far removed from the marked structure in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fornix is a white matter tract of the limbic system, responsible for connecting the hippocampus to other brain regions, and is located beneath the corpus callosum in a mid-sagittal view of the brain.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: The cell marked in the below slide is inhibitory to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Deep nuclei of cerebellum

 

The cell marked in the histological slide is a Purkinje cell, a large, distinctive neuron found in the cerebellar cortex.

 

  • Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and their axons project to the deep cerebellar nuclei, such as the dentate, interposed, and fastigial nuclei.
  • Purkinje cells release GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), an inhibitory neurotransmitter, which inhibits the activity of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
  • This inhibition plays a critical role in fine-tuning motor coordination and maintaining balance.

 

Thus, the Purkinje cell is inhibitory to the deep nuclei of the cerebellum, which process cerebellar output to other parts of the brain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vestibular nuclei: While the cerebellum sends information to the vestibular nuclei to assist in maintaining balance and posture, Purkinje cells do not directly inhibit the vestibular nuclei.

 

Option C. Inferior olivary nucleus: The inferior olivary nucleus provides climbing fibers to Purkinje cells, facilitating their activity. It is not inhibited by Purkinje cells.

 

Option D. Basal ganglia: The basal ganglia are involved in motor control and do not receive input from Purkinje cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex are inhibitory to the deep nuclei of the cerebellum, fine-tuning motor coordination and balance through GABAergic neurotransmission.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: What is the blood supply of the structure marked in the image below?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

options.label: D
options.text: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

questions.answerText: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

 

The corpus callosum is primarily supplied by branches of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), which is connected by the anterior communicating artery (AComA).

 

  • Anterior cerebral artery (ACA):
    • Supplies most of the corpus callosum, including the genu and body.
    • It also supplies medial portions of the frontal and parietal lobes.
  • Anterior communicating artery (AComA):
    • This artery connects the left and right anterior cerebral arteries and contributes to the vascular supply of the anterior portions of the corpus callosum, particularly the rostrum and genu.

 

Thus, the combination of the anterior cerebral artery and the anterior communicating artery is responsible for supplying the structure marked in the image.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery supplies lateral cortical regions and does not contribute to the corpus callosum’s blood supply.

 

Option B. Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the splenium of the corpus callosum, not the anterior portions.

 

Option D. Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery does not supply the corpus callosum, and this combination is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The corpus callosum, particularly its anterior portions (rostrum and genu), is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery and the anterior communicating artery.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: At which level does the nerve supply for the marked muscle arise?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Red nucleus

 

The marked muscle in the image is the medial rectus, which is responsible for adduction of the eyeball (moving it inward). The medial rectus is supplied by the third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve). The nucleus of the third cranial nerve is located at the level of the superior colliculus of the midbrain, where the red nucleus is also present.

 

The red nucleus is a distinctive, iron-containing structure found at this level in the midbrain and serves as a key anatomical landmark.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Subthalamic nuclei: The subthalamic nucleus is part of the basal ganglia and is involved in motor control, not in the cranial nerve supply to muscles. It is located in the diencephalon and does not relate to the medial rectus or its nerve supply.

 

Option C. Decussation of pyramidal tract: The decussation of the pyramidal tract occurs at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord, primarily involving the crossing over of motor fibers. It has no connection to the third cranial nerve or the medial rectus.

 

Option D. Olivary nucleus: The olivary nucleus is a structure in the medulla involved in motor learning and coordination. It does not play a role in the innervation of the medial rectus muscle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial rectus muscle is supplied by the third cranial nerve, whose nucleus is located at the level of the superior colliculus in the midbrain, near the red nucleus.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: During climbing the staircase, a person suddenly fell & a sharp object hit on his neck. After the injury, the patient is unable to shrug/ elevate the shoulder & he is having difficulty in turning his head. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Spinal Accessory nerve

 

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) is primarily responsible for innervating the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Damage to this nerve typically results in:

 

  • Inability to shrug or elevate the shoulder due to loss of trapezius function.
  • Difficulty turning the head to the opposite side, as the sternocleidomastoid assists in head rotation.

 

In this case, the sharp object likely injured the spinal accessory nerve, causing these characteristic deficits.

 

The trapezius muscle, which is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve, has an upper fiber responsible for scapular elevation. The inability to shrug is a hallmark sign of trapezius dysfunction. Similarly, the sternocleidomastoid aids in head rotation and neck flexion, further implicating the spinal accessory nerve when its function is impaired.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Long thoracic nerve: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior muscle, which is responsible for protracting and stabilizing the scapula. Damage to this nerve results in a "winged scapula," not difficulty in shrugging the shoulder or turning the head.

 

Option C. Sternocleidomastoid: While the sternocleidomastoid is involved in turning the head, it is not directly implicated as the primary structure in this injury. Instead, its dysfunction is due to spinal accessory nerve damage, which supplies it.

 

Option D. Deltoid: The deltoid muscle is innervated by the axillary nerve and is responsible for shoulder abduction. Damage to the deltoid or its nerve supply would not result in difficulty shrugging the shoulder or head rotation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) innervates the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles. Injury to this nerve leads to an inability to shrug the shoulder and difficulty turning the head.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A patient presented with swelling below the ear & complained of pain in the lobule of the ear. He is having difficulty in eating food. What nerve is most likely to be damaged?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Greater Auricular nerve

 

The greater auricular nerve supplies the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible, and the lobule of the ear. Pain and swelling in these areas are characteristic of irritation or damage to this nerve, often associated with conditions affecting the parotid region, such as infections, trauma, or surgical complications.

 

In this patient, the swelling below the ear and pain in the lobule strongly suggest involvement of the greater auricular nerve, as it innervates these regions. The patient’s difficulty eating may be due to associated pain or discomfort from swelling in the parotid region.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Auriculotemporal nerve: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. It provides sensory innervation to the anterior part of the external ear and the temporal region. While it is involved in conditions like Frey's syndrome and parotid gland-related issues, it does not typically cause pain localized to the ear lobule or swelling below the ear.

 

Option C. Facial nerve: The facial nerve primarily provides motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and does not supply sensory fibers to the lobule of the ear. Damage to the facial nerve would result in motor deficits such as facial weakness or paralysis, which are not present in this case.

 

Option D. Vagus/Inferior alveolar nerve: The vagus nerve and the inferior alveolar nerve are unrelated to the sensory innervation of the lobule of the ear. The vagus nerve is primarily involved in autonomic functions and some sensory innervation of the external ear, but not the lobule specifically. The inferior alveolar nerve is involved in the innervation of the teeth and chin, not the ear.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The greater auricular nerve is the primary sensory nerve supplying the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible, and the ear lobule. Damage or irritation to this nerve causes pain and swelling in these regions.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A man suffered an injury on head and after this the blood collected around the eyes. Which of the following layer is responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Loose areolar layer

 

The loose areolar tissue layer is the fourth layer of the scalp, lying between the aponeurotic layer and the periosteum. This layer is often referred to as the "dangerous area of the scalp" because it is loosely attached and provides a potential space for blood or infections to spread.

 

In the case of a head injury, blood can collect in the loose areolar layer. This layer does not have any bony attachment on the anterior side, allowing blood to track anteriorly and accumulate around the eyes, causing the characteristic discoloration referred to as a "black eye," "panda sign," or "raccoon eye."

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Periosteum: The periosteum (or pericranium) is the innermost layer of the scalp and is closely adhered to the skull. While it plays a role in head injuries, it does not allow for blood to spread anteriorly to the eyes because it is tightly bound to the bone, limiting its role in such conditions.

 

Option B. Aponeurotic layer: The aponeurotic layer (galea aponeurotica) is the third layer of the scalp, connecting the frontalis and occipitalis muscles. It is not involved in allowing blood to spread to the eyes after an injury because it is firmly attached to surrounding tissues.

 

Option D. Connective tissue layer: The connective tissue layer is the second layer of the scalp, which is dense and contains blood vessels and nerves. While it is involved in scalp injuries, it does not have the anatomical characteristics required for blood to collect around the eyes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The loose areolar layer of the scalp is responsible for the spread of blood to the periorbital region following head injuries, resulting in a "black eye" or "raccoon eye." This layer's loose attachment and lack of anterior bony attachment make it a key site for blood accumulation.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following is a direct content of cavernous sinus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Abducent nerve

 

The cavernous sinus is a dural venous sinus located on either side of the sella turcica. It has a unique arrangement of structures passing through it or along its walls.

 

Direct Contents of the Cavernous Sinus:

 

  1. Abducent nerve (CN VI): The only cranial nerve that runs through the sinus itself, close to the internal carotid artery.
  2. Internal carotid artery: Courses through the sinus, surrounded by the carotid plexus.

 

Structures in the Lateral Wall of the Cavernous Sinus:

 

  1. Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
  2. Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
  3. Ophthalmic branch (V1) of the trigeminal nerve
  4. Maxillary branch (V2) of the trigeminal nerve

 

These nerves lie in the lateral wall but do not directly course within the sinus cavity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Oculomotor nerve: Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not within the sinus itself.

 

Option B. Trochlear nerve: Incorrect. The trochlear nerve also lies in the lateral wall, not as a direct content within the sinus cavity.

 

Option C. Maxillary branch of trigeminal: Incorrect. The maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve (V2) runs in the lateral wall, outside the sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The abducent nerve (CN VI) and internal carotid artery are the only direct contents of the cavernous sinus, while other cranial nerves lie in its lateral wall.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a complaint of dragging his foot while walking. On examination, he demonstrates difficulty in dorsiflexing his foot at the ankle. This clinical presentation is most likely due to a lesion affecting which nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Deep Peroneal (Fibular) Nerve

 

The clinical presentation of foot drop is characterized by the inability to dorsiflex the foot at the ankle. This condition is typically caused by injury or dysfunction of the deep peroneal nerve, which innervates the muscles responsible for dorsiflexion:

 

  1. Tibialis anterior: Main dorsiflexor of the foot.
  2. Extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus: Assist in dorsiflexion and toe extension.

 

The deep peroneal nerve is a branch of the common peroneal (fibular) nerve and runs in the anterior compartment of the leg. Lesions can occur due to trauma, compression, or neuropathy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sciatic Nerve: Incorrect. While the sciatic nerve branches into the common peroneal nerve and the tibial nerve, a lesion here would cause more extensive motor and sensory loss, not isolated foot drop.

 

Option C. Tibial Nerve: Incorrect. The tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg, responsible for plantarflexion. A lesion here would impair plantarflexion, not dorsiflexion.

 

Option D. Sural Nerve: Incorrect. The sural nerve is a sensory nerve providing sensation to the posterior and lateral aspects of the leg and foot. It has no role in motor function or dorsiflexion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Foot drop, characterized by the inability to dorsiflex the foot, is due to dysfunction of the deep peroneal nerve, which innervates the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: During embryonic development, the aortic arches play a crucial role in forming the major arteries of the head and neck region. The third aortic arch contributes to the formation of which important blood vessel?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Common carotid artery

 

The third aortic arch plays a crucial role in the development of the following major arteries:

 

  1. Proximal Part: Forms the common carotid artery (both right and left).
  2. Distal Part: Forms the proximal segment of the internal carotid artery.

 

The external carotid artery develops as a branch of the common carotid artery, and the vertebral artery is unrelated to the third aortic arch.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Internal carotid artery: Partially correct but not complete. The proximal segment of the internal carotid artery is derived from the third aortic arch. The rest of the internal carotid artery forms from the dorsal aorta.

 

Option C. External carotid artery: Incorrect. The external carotid artery arises as a sprouting branch from the common carotid artery, not directly from the third aortic arch.

 

Option D. Vertebral artery: Incorrect. The vertebral artery develops from the dorsal intersegmental arteries, not from any aortic arch.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The third aortic arch forms:

 

  • The common carotid artery (proximal part).
  • The proximal internal carotid artery (distal part).
    It does not directly contribute to the external carotid or vertebral arteries.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with pain and tenderness over the right clavicle. Physical examination reveals localized swelling and crepitus upon palpation. Radiological imaging shows a midshaft clavicle fracture. Which anatomical structure is most commonly affected in this type of fracture?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Middle third of the clavicle

 

The clavicle is commonly divided into three anatomical segments: the medial third, middle third, and lateral third. 

 

According to Allman orthopedic classifications, approximately 85% of fractures occur at the middle third of the clavicle, making this the most frequently affected area in clavicular fractures. This is due to the fact that the middle third is the weakest part of the bone and is subjected to the most stress during physical trauma. 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sternoclavicular joint: This joint is located at the medial end of the clavicle, where it articulates with the sternum. Fractures in the midshaft region of the clavicle are distant from this joint, so it is typically not involved in midshaft fractures. The sternoclavicular joint is involved more with injuries affecting the medial third of the clavicle.

 

Option B.  Acromioclavicular joint: This joint is located at the lateral end of the clavicle, where the clavicle meets the acromion of the scapula. It is also distant from the midshaft of the clavicle and is usually involved in lateral third clavicle injuries, rather than midshaft fractures.

 

Option C. Coracoclavicular ligaments: These ligaments stabilize the clavicle by connecting it to the coracoid process of the scapula. While these ligaments may be affected in fractures of the lateral third of the clavicle, they are typically not involved in midshaft fractures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The middle third of the clavicle is the most common site for clavicle fractures, accounting for approximately 85% of cases. This is a key anatomical fact that should be remembered when dealing with trauma to the clavicular region.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements regarding the marked structure is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It is example of pressure epiphysis.

options.label: B
options.text: It gives attachment to long head of humerus and coracobrachialis.

options.label: C
options.text: It is palpable in delto-pectoral groove.

options.label: D
options.text: It is not palpable in infraclavicular fossa even in thin built persons.

questions.answerText: It is palpable in delto-pectoral groove.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is palpable in delto-pectoral groove

 

The coracoid process of the scapula is the marked structure in this question. It is a bony prominence that serves as an attachment site for several muscles, including the short head of the biceps brachii and the coracobrachialis. 

 

The coracoid process can be palpated in the delto-pectoral groove, which is the anatomical space between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles. This is an important clinical landmark used during examinations to locate the coracoid process, especially in patients with shoulder injuries.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is example of pressure epiphysis: This is incorrect because the coracoid process is an example of an atavistic epiphysis, meaning it was once a separate bone during development but later fused with the scapula. A pressure epiphysis, on the other hand, refers to areas of bone subjected to pressure during growth, such as the head of the humerus.

 

Option B.  It gives attachment to long head of humerus and coracobrachialis: This is incorrect. The coracoid process provides attachment to the short head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis muscles, not the long head of the biceps or the humerus.

 

Option D. It is not palpable in infraclavicular fossa even in thin built persons: This statement is incorrect. The coracoid process is generally palpable in the infraclavicular fossa, especially in individuals with a thin build. It is located below the lateral third of the clavicle and can be palpated easily.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The coracoid process is a palpable structure found in the delto-pectoral groove and serves as an attachment site for the short head of the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following clinical statements are true? A. Congenital absence of pectoralis major is known as Poland syndrome.B. Due to damage of Bell’s nerve (long thoracic nerve), winging of scapula occurs.C. Congenital high scapula is also known as Sprengel's deformity.D. In Cleidocranial dysostosis, clavicle is absent and shoulders can be approximated.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A, B, C, D

 

A. Poland syndrome is a congenital condition where there is an absence or underdevelopment of the pectoralis major muscle on one side of the body, leading to visible deformity is a classical feature of Poland syndrome.

 

 

B.  Winging of the scapula occurs due to damage to the long thoracic nerve (also known as Bell’s nerve). This nerve supplies the serratus anterior muscle, which stabilizes the scapula. When the nerve is damaged, the scapula protrudes, leading to a winging appearance.

 

 

C. Congenital high scapula is indeed known as Sprengel's deformity. It is a rare congenital disorder where one of the scapulae is positioned higher than the other, often leading to a reduced range of motion in the shoulder.

 

 

D. Cleidocranial dysostosis is a genetic disorder characterized by absent or underdeveloped clavicles, which allows the shoulders to be approximated or brought closer together, a unique feature of this condition.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Poland syndrome involves underdevelopment of the pectoralis major, causing noticeable asymmetry. Winging of the scapula results from long thoracic nerve damage, leading to protrusion. Sprengel's deformity and cleidocranial dysostosis present with distinctive skeletal abnormalities that affect shoulder structure and mobility.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old software engineer presents to the clinic complaining of chronic neck pain and stiffness. The pain is localized on the back and side of the neck and sometimes radiates to the shoulder. The patient reports that the pain worsens after long periods of working on the computer. Physical examination reveals tenderness and tightness in the upper neck region. Pain is particularly exacerbated by rotating the head to the opposite side and tilting it downwards. Marked muscle is most likely involved in this patient's condition. What is the nerve supply of this muscle?

options.label: C
options.text: From the dorsal rami of C1

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Dorsal scapular nerve

 

The levator scapulae is the muscle most likely involved in this patient's symptoms of neck pain and stiffness, especially given the history of posture-related strain and the physical exam findings of pain upon neck rotation and tilting. The levator scapulae elevates the scapula and rotates the neck. It is innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5), which also innervates the rhomboid muscles. This nerve originates from the brachial plexus and is responsible for the motor function of these muscles, which can become tight or strained in individuals with poor posture, especially those who work long hours at a computer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Suprascapular nerve: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, which are primarily involved in abduction and external rotation of the arm. This nerve is unrelated to the levator scapulae and its functions, making it an incorrect option.

 

Option C. From the dorsal rami of C1: The dorsal rami of C1, also known as the suboccipital nerve, innervates muscles of the suboccipital triangle, including the rectus capitis posterior and obliquus capitis muscles. These muscles are primarily responsible for movements of the head, not scapular elevation, so this is incorrect for the levator scapulae.

 

Option D. Subscapular nerve: The subscapular nerve innervates the subscapularis muscle, part of the rotator cuff. This muscle is responsible for internal rotation of the shoulder joint and is not involved in scapular elevation or neck movement. Therefore, it is not relevant to this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The levator scapulae muscle, involved in neck elevation and movement, is innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5), and its strain is often associated with neck pain and stiffness due to poor posture or overuse.
