questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of these is not a type of synovial joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Symphysis pubis

 

The symphysis pubis is classified as a secondary cartilaginous joint (also known as an amphiarthrosis), not a synovial joint. In this type of joint, the bones are united by fibrocartilage, allowing for limited movement. In the case of the symphysis pubis, the fibrocartilage is located between the two pubic bones.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Costotransverse joint: This is a plane synovial joint between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process of the vertebra, allowing for slight gliding movements, especially during respiration.

 

Option B.  Costovertebral joint: The costovertebral joint is a plane synovial joint formed between the head of the rib and the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae. Like the costotransverse joint, it contributes to rib movements during breathing.

 

Option C. Radiocarpal joint: The radiocarpal joint, commonly known as the wrist joint, is a synovial joint (ellipsoid type), which allows for flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction of the hand.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which among the following is incorrect regarding Sibson's fascia?

options.label: A
options.text: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

questions.answerText: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

 

Sibson's fascia, also known as the suprapleural membrane, is a dense fascial layer that covers the apex of the lung and acts as a barrier between the neck and the thoracic cavity. It is attached to the inner border of the 1st rib, not the 2nd rib, This fascial structure provides protection for vital structures, such as the subclavian artery and vein, which pass above it.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Covers apical part of lung: This is correct. Sibson's fascia extends over the apex of the lung, providing protection and structure to the area.

 

Option C. Part of scalenus minimus muscle: This is correct. Sibson's fascia is often considered a derivative of the scalenus minimus muscle, a small muscle that may be present in some individuals and is involved in respiration.

 

Option D. Vessels pass above the fascia: This is correct. The subclavian artery and vein pass above Sibson's fascia, confirming the relationship of the fascia to these major vessels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sibson's fascia is attached to the inner border of the 1st rib, covers the apex of the lung, and plays a role in protecting the structures in the thoracic inlet, with vessels such as the subclavian artery and vein passing above it .

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the cartilage shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) White fibrocartilage

 

The image shows fibrocartilage/ White fibrocartilage, which is characterized by thick, red, wavy bundles of collagen fibers visible between the rows of chondrocytes. Fibrocartilage is a tough, dense type of cartilage that provides both rigidity and flexibility. The collagen bundles provide strength, making fibrocartilage the type of cartilage found in intervertebral discs and other areas where both flexibility and tensile strength are needed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Non articular hyaline cartilage: This type of cartilage is found in the trachea, bronchi, and the nose. It appears more glassy with a smooth matrix lacking the thick collagen fibers seen in fibrocartilage.

 

Option B.  Articular hyaline cartilage: Articular hyaline cartilage covers the surfaces of bones in synovial joints. It lacks the wavy collagen bundles seen in fibrocartilage and instead has a smooth, glassy appearance with more evenly distributed chondrocytes.

 

Option C. Yellow cartilage: Also known as elastic cartilage, yellow cartilage contains elastic fibers, which give it flexibility. It is found in structures like the external ear and epiglottis, and its appearance is distinct from fibrocartilage due to the presence of elastic fibers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

White fibrocartilage is recognized by its thick, wavy bundles of collagen and is found in structures that require strength and the ability to withstand compression, such as intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis

 

Additional Information

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: During a yawn, a student experienced a jaw locking incident. Identify the muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lateral pterygoid

 

The lateral pterygoid muscle is the only muscle that attaches directly to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). It plays an essential role in protracting the mandible (moving it forward) and is also involved in depressing the mandible (opening the mouth). During yawning, this muscle contracts, pulling the articular disc forward to allow for smooth movement of the mandible. If there is dysfunction or overactivity in the lateral pterygoid muscle, it can lead to jaw locking, as seen in this student's case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B.  Temporalis: The temporalis muscle is primarily responsible for elevation and retraction of the mandible. It does not attach to the articular disc and is involved in closing the jaw.

 

Option C. Medial pterygoid: The medial pterygoid muscle assists in elevation and side-to-side movements of the mandible but does not attach to the articular disc.

 

Option D. Masseter: The masseter muscle is involved in elevation (closing the mouth) and plays a role in chewing, but it does not attach to the articular disc.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle that attaches to the articular disc of the TMJ and is responsible for protracting the mandible, which can lead to jaw locking if it malfunctions​

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Injury to the nerve that lies medially to the structure pointed will result in:

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from posterior 1/3 tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from posterior most part of tongue

questions.answerText: Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

 

The nerve that lies medially to the structure pointed in the image is the chorda tympani, which is a branch of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). This nerve is responsible for providing taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. If this nerve is injured, the patient would lose the ability to perceive taste in this portion of the tongue.

 

The chorda tympani courses medially to the spine of the sphenoid and enters the infratemporal fossa, where it joins the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve) to supply the taste fibers to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

 

Other Options:


Option B. Loss of taste sensation from posterior 1/3 tongue: This function is provided by the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX), not the chorda tympani, so this option is incorrect.
 

Option C. Loss of general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue: General sensation (not taste) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve (cranial nerve V3), and is not affected by an injury to the chorda tympani.
 

Option D. Loss of taste sensation from posterior most part of tongue: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) provides taste sensation to the posterior most part of the tongue, not the chorda tympani.

 

Educational Objective:


Injury to the chorda tympani results in the loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the papillae from the given histological section:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Circumvallate

 

Circumvallate papillae are large, circular papillae located towards the back of the tongue. They are characterized by their circular structure with a surrounding trench,. These papillae contain numerous taste buds, particularly located in the trenches. They are important for taste sensation and are easily identifiable in histological sections due to their size and distinct trench appearance. The circumvallate papillae also have a unique arrangement that forms a V-shape on the posterior tongue.

 

 

Other Options:


Option A. Fungiform: These papillae are smaller and mushroom-shaped, scattered across the surface of the tongue. They are not characterized by the trenches seen in circumvallate papillae.
 

Option C. Filiform: These are thread-like papillae found on the surface of the tongue. They are keratinized and do not contain taste buds, and they present with a pointed appearance in histological sections.
 

Option D. Foliate: These papillae have a leaf-like appearance with parallel ridges on the lateral sides of the tongue. They are more prominent in some animals and are rudimentary in humans.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Circumvallate papillae are large, circular structures with surrounding trenches, located at the back of the tongue, and they are heavily involved in taste sensation.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the nerve root(s) of the thickened nerve marked in the arrow in the image shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) C2, C3
 

The thickened nerve marked in the image is the great auricular nerve, which provides sensory innervation to the skin around the ear and over the parotid gland. The great auricular nerve arises from the C2 and C3 nerve roots of the cervical plexus and travels upwards towards the auricle of the ear. It is commonly implicated in clinical conditions that affect the region of the neck and ear, and its enlargement can sometimes be observed in certain pathological conditions.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. C1: The C1 nerve root primarily contributes to the cervical plexus and does not form the great auricular nerve.
 

Option B. C2: While C2 is one of the nerve roots involved in forming the great auricular nerve, it is not sufficient on its own to form this nerve without C3.
 

Option C. C1, C2: This combination does not form the great auricular nerve, as C3 is essential for its formation.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The great auricular nerve is formed by the C2 and C3 nerve roots, and it provides sensory innervation to the area around the ear and parotid region.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: In the image, identify the longest muscle in the human body, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial knee, crossing both the hip and knee joints. This muscle acts as a flexor, abductor, and lateral rotator of the hip and a flexor of the knee, playing a vital role in activities like sitting cross-legged.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A


The sartorius muscle is the longest muscle (45 cm) in the human body, running from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the medial side of the knee. It crosses both the hip and knee joints and is involved in multiple movements, including flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation of the hip and flexion of the knee. This muscle is particularly important in allowing the leg to assume the cross-legged position, also known as the "tailor's" or "lotus" position.

 

Other Options:
 

Option B. B refers to the rectus femoris, a quadriceps muscle primarily responsible for extending the knee.
 

Option C. C represents the vastus lateralis, which also extends the knee but does not cross the hip joint.
 

Option D. D is likely the tensor fasciae latae, which assists in hip abduction but is not the longest muscle in the body.

 

Educational Objective:
 

The sartorius muscle is the longest muscle in the human body, and it is involved in flexing, abducting, and laterally rotating the hip while also flexing the knee.

Option D. D is likely the tensor fasciae latae, which assists in hip abduction but is not the longest muscle in the body. questions.stemHtml: Choose the correct option for the below image:

options.label: A
options.text: A – Neural tube, B – Presomite mesoderm, C - Ectoderm, D - Somite

options.label: B
options.text: A – Neural tube, B – Presomite mesoderm, C - Mesoderm, D - Somite

options.label: C
options.text: A – Neural tube, B – Somite, C - Ectoderm, D - Presomite mesoderm

options.label: D
options.text: A – Neural tube, B – Somite, C - Mesoderm, D - Presomite mesoderm

questions.answerText: A – Neural tube, B – Somite, C - Ectoderm, D - Presomite mesoderm
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) A – Neural tube, B – Somite, C - Ectoderm, D - Presomite mesoderm


In the provided image of an early-stage embryo, the labeled structures correspond to key components of early embryonic development. The neural tube is the central structure forming from the ectoderm, which will develop into the central nervous system. On either side of the neural tube are the somites, segmented blocks of mesoderm that contribute to the development of the vertebrae, muscles, and dermis. The ectoderm surrounds these structures, forming the outermost layer of the embryo, while the presomite mesoderm is the area where future somites will form.

 

In the image, ectoderm has been removed from the area where the neural tube is visible and the zig zag pattern seen along the structure marked C is the exact site from where the ectoderm has been removed to view the underlying neural tube.

 

Educational Objective:
 

In early embryonic development, the neural tube forms the central nervous system, the somites contribute to the musculoskeletal system, and the ectoderm is the outer layer from which the neural tube arises.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) A-anterior communicating artery, B-ICA, C-Infundibulum, D-posterior communicating artery, E-III nerve, F- IV nerve


The provided structures correspond to key elements in the Circle of Willis and related anatomical features:

 

A (Anterior communicating artery): This artery connects the left and right anterior cerebral arteries.

 

B (ICA - Internal carotid artery): One of the major arteries supplying the brain, entering the Circle of Willis.

 

C (Infundibulum): The pituitary stalk, connecting the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus, lies in this area.

 

D (Posterior communicating artery): This artery connects the internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral arteries, completing the Circle of Willis.

 

E (III Nerve - Oculomotor nerve): The third cranial nerve, which controls most of the eye movements, passes close to the Circle of Willis.

 

F (IV Nerve - Trochlear nerve): The fourth cranial nerve, which innervates the superior oblique muscle of the eye, is located posteriorly.

 

Circle of Willis 

 

 

Educational Objective:


The structures near the Circle of Willis are vital in supplying blood to the brain, with key arteries like the anterior communicating artery, internal carotid artery, and posterior communicating artery playing crucial roles.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 32-year-old male presents with weakness and numbness in his right arm following a motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals decreased sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm and weakness of elbow flexion. Which part of the brachial plexus does not give branches?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Division

 

The brachial plexus is organized into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches. Divisions of the brachial plexus do not give off any branches. The divisions are formed from the splitting of the trunks into anterior and posterior divisions, which then unite to form the cords. It is at the level of the cords and roots where branches arise that innervate various parts of the upper limb, but the divisions serve primarily as passageways without branching out into nerves.  It is the only part of the brachial plexus that does not give off branches.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Roots: The roots of the brachial plexus do give off branches, including the dorsal scapular nerve and the long thoracic nerve, which innervate muscles such as the rhomboids and serratus anterior.
 

Option B. Trunks: The upper trunk of the brachial plexus gives off the suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius. These branches innervate important muscles in the shoulder region.
 

Option D. Cords: The cords of the brachial plexus give off several important branches, including the lateral pectoral nerve, the medial pectoral nerve, and the thoracodorsal nerve, which are crucial for upper limb innervation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The divisions of the brachial plexus do not give rise to any branches, unlike the roots, trunks, and cords, which all contribute branches to various nerves of the upper limb.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 40-year-old male presents to the primary care clinic with lower back pain radiating down his left leg. He reports a history of heavy lifting at work. On physical examination, there is tenderness over the lumbar vertebrae with limited lumbar spine flexion due to pain. Which anatomical curvature is normally observed in the lumbar spine?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lordosis

 

 

The normal curvature of the lumbar spine is lordosis, which refers to the inward (concave) curvature of the spine in the lumbar region. This curvature helps to maintain balance and absorb shock during activities such as walking and lifting. In the image provided, we can clearly observe the lumbar region exhibiting lordosis with an angle of about 45°. This is a physiological curvature essential for proper posture and spinal function.

 

In cases of lower back pain, especially related to heavy lifting, the lumbar lordosis can be strained, leading to discomfort and pain, as seen in the patient's symptoms.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option B. Scoliosis refers to an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine.

 

Option C. Kyphosis is the outward curvature typically found in the thoracic spine (a posterior convex curve).

 

Option D. Recurvatum refers to hyperextension, typically associated with joints, particularly the knee, and is not related to the curvature of the spine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The normal curvature of the lumbar spine is lordosis, which helps with weight distribution and maintaining proper posture.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Arrange the given stages of spermatogenesis in the correct sequence: A. SpermatidB. SpermatozoaC. SpermatogoniumD. Spermatocyte
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C → D → A → B

 

Spermatogenesis is the process by which sperm cells are produced and developed in the testes. The correct sequence of stages in spermatogenesis is as follows:

 

C. Spermatogonium: These are the diploid stem cells located in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. They divide by mitosis to give rise to primary spermatocytes.

 

D. Spermatocyte: The spermatogonium differentiates into spermatocytes (primary and secondary), which undergo meiosis to produce haploid cells known as spermatids.

 

A. Spermatid: After meiosis, the resulting spermatids are round haploid cells that undergo further maturation.

 

B. Spermatozoa: The spermatids mature into spermatozoa (mature sperm cells), which are then capable of fertilizing an egg.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of spermatogenesis is Spermatogonium → Spermatocyte → Spermatid → Spermatozoa.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A patient developed the following deformity after overhead weightlifting & pushing exercises. Which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Serratus anterior

 

The image shows a winged scapula, a condition commonly caused by injury or weakness of the serratus anterior muscle. This muscle is responsible for holding the scapula against the thoracic wall. It is innervated by the long thoracic nerve, which is vulnerable during overhead lifting or pushing exercises.

 

When the serratus anterior is weak or paralyzed, the medial border of the scapula protrudes outward, causing the characteristic winging seen in this patient. This condition typically arises when the long thoracic nerve is injured, such as during excessive or improper overhead weight-lifting activities.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Latissimus dorsi: This muscle is involved in shoulder adduction, extension, and internal rotation, but it does not stabilize the scapula against the ribcage.
 

Option B. Trapezius: Although the trapezius plays a role in scapular movement, damage to this muscle does not result in a winged scapula.
 

Option D. Supraspinatus: This muscle is part of the rotator cuff and helps with shoulder abduction but is not involved in scapular stabilization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Weakness or injury to the serratus anterior muscle, typically due to damage to the long thoracic nerve, leads to a winged scapula.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: The tissue in the image is found in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Epiphyseal plates

 

The tissue in the image is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, which is present in epiphyseal plates (growth plates). Hyaline cartilage is known for its glassy, smooth appearance and its role in bone growth during childhood and adolescence. The chondrocytes, seen within lacunae, are embedded in a matrix that provides support and flexibility to the developing bone.

 

 

Epiphyseal plates are responsible for longitudinal bone growth. They are present between the diaphysis and epiphysis of long bones and are essential for bone elongation during development.

 

The matrix of hyaline cartilage stains pink with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain, which is consistent with the features of epiphyseal plate cartilage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Articular disc: The articular disc contains fibrocartilage, which has a more fibrous appearance and is found in joints like the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).

 

Option B. Intervertebral disc: The intervertebral disc consists of fibrocartilage in the annulus fibrosus, which does not resemble the hyaline cartilage

 

Option D. Pinna of ear: The pinna contains elastic cartilage, which has a different structure characterized by the presence of elastic fibers 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The tissue in the image is hyaline cartilage, which is typically found in epiphyseal plates, where it plays a crucial role in bone growth.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: The pointed structure supplies all the following parts of the conducting system in the heart:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) SA node

 

The pointed structure in the image is the right coronary artery. The right coronary artery primarily supplies blood to the SA node (sinoatrial node) and part of the right atrium. It is also responsible for supplying the AV node in most individuals, but it does not supply the AV bundle (bundle of His) or the left bundle branch, which are mainly supplied by the left coronary artery and its branches.

 

The right coronary artery arises from the right aortic sinus and runs along the atrioventricular groove, giving off branches like the SA nodal branch.

 

The AV bundle and left bundle branch are primarily supplied by the left anterior descending artery, which is a branch of the left coronary artery.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. AV bundle: The AV bundle is supplied by the left anterior descending artery and not the right coronary artery.

 

Option C. Left bundle branch: The left bundle branch is supplied by the left anterior descending artery as well.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The right coronary artery supplies the SA node and parts of the AV node, but it does not supply the AV bundle or the left bundle branch.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Injury to the artery that lies beneath the arrow will lead to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Extradural hemorrhage

 

The arrow in the image is pointing to the pterion, a region where several cranial bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid) meet. Just beneath this area lies the middle meningeal artery, which is vulnerable to injury in cases of trauma to the lateral skull, such as a blow to the head.

 

If the middle meningeal artery is ruptured, it leads to an extradural (epidural) hemorrhage, characterized by the accumulation of blood between the dura mater and the skull. This is often associated with a lucid interval followed by rapid neurological deterioration if not treated promptly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Subarachnoid haemorrhage: This occurs due to bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from a ruptured aneurysm or trauma to vessels in that space and is not associated with damage to the middle meningeal artery.

 

Option C. Subdural hemorrhage: Subdural hemorrhage results from tearing of bridging veins between the dura and arachnoid mater, typically in cases of shearing injury, not from injury to the middle meningeal artery.

 

Option D. Intraparenchymal haemorrhage: This refers to bleeding within the brain tissue itself, which is often caused by hypertension or trauma but does not involve the middle meningeal artery.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Injury to the middle meningeal artery located beneath the pterion can cause an extradural hemorrhage, a life-threatening condition that requires immediate medical attention.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pivot joint

 

Supination and pronation of the forearm occur at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, both of which are examples of pivot joints. These joints allow the radius to rotate around the ulna, facilitating the movements of supination (turning the palm upward) and pronation (turning the palm downward). A pivot joint permits rotation around a single axis, making it ideal for such rotational movements.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Saddle joint: Saddle joints allow for movement in two planes, such as in the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb, but they are not involved in rotation like supination and pronation.

 

Option C. Ellipsoid joint: Also known as a condyloid joint, this type of joint allows movement in two planes (flexion-extension and abduction-adduction), but not rotation.

 

Option D. Ball and socket joint: These joints, such as the shoulder and hip joints, allow for movement in multiple planes, including rotation, but they are not involved in forearm supination and pronation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pivot joints, such as the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, are responsible for the rotational movements of supination and pronation in the forearm.

questions.stem: For the conjoint tendon, all are true except?

options.label: A
options.text: Formed by the internal oblique aponeurosis and transversus abdominis aponeurosis

options.label: B
options.text: Forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal

options.label: C
options.text: Protects the superficial inguinal ring to maintain the integrity of the inguinal canal

options.label: D
options.text: Runs parallel to the inguinal ligament

questions.answerText: Runs parallel to the inguinal ligament
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Runs parallel to the inguinal ligament

 

The conjoint tendon is formed by the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. It plays a key role in forming the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and provides protection to the superficial inguinal ring to help maintain the canal's structural integrity. The incorrect statement is that the conjoint tendon "runs parallel to the inguinal ligament," which it does not.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Formed by the internal oblique aponeurosis and transversus abdominis aponeurosis: This is correct; the conjoint tendon is made from these two aponeuroses.
 

Option B. Forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal: This is accurate; the conjoint tendon forms a crucial part of the posterior wall.
 

Option C. Protects the superficial inguinal ring to maintain the integrity of the inguinal canal: Correct; this is another vital function of the conjoint tendon.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The conjoint tendon forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and is made up of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, but it does not run parallel to the inguinal ligament.

Ans. A) 1- liver, 2- pancreas, 3- spleen

The image correctly identifies the liver, pancreas, and spleen as structures 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

questions.stemHtml: The marked line corresponds to which vertebral level?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) L3

 

The marked line corresponds to the L3 vertebral level. Clinically, the line drawn between the highest points of the iliac crests is often used as a reference point to identify the L3-L4 vertebral interspace. This level is crucial, particularly for procedures such as lumbar punctures, as it provides a safe entry point to avoid damage to the spinal cord, which usually ends at the L1-L2 level in adults.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. T12: T12 is located at the thoracolumbar junction, much higher than the line shown in the image.


Option B. L1: While L1 is closer, the line of the iliac crests is generally below this vertebra.


Option C. L2: L2 is near, but the iliac crest line more commonly intersects at the L3 level, which is more commonly used as a landmark.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The iliac crest line is a reliable landmark for identifying the L3 vertebral level, important in procedures like lumbar puncture.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked chamber.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Left atrium


In the given image, the marked chamber corresponds to the left atrium. The left atrium is located posteriorly in the heart and is part of the systemic circulation where oxygenated blood from the lungs enters before being pumped into the left ventricle. The anatomy of the left atrium is such that it forms part of the posterior surface of the heart, which is visible in radiographic views.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Right atrium: The right atrium is positioned on the right border of the heart and is responsible for receiving deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation, not the marked structure in the image.
 

Option C. Right ventricle: The right ventricle forms the anterior surface of the heart and is not the chamber marked in this image.
 

Option D. Left ventricle: While the left ventricle is located near the left atrium, it is typically more inferior and anterior, and does not correspond to the marked structure.

 

Educational objectives:


The left atrium, located posteriorly in the heart, is the chamber marked in this image and plays a key role in receiving oxygenated blood from the lungs.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 62-year-old patient was brought to the ER following a suspected stroke. The patient was unable to speak fluently, though he understands the given instructions. Which category of aphasia is most likely present in the patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Broca’s aphasia

 

Broca’s aphasia, also known as non-fluent aphasia, is characterized by the patient's inability to speak fluently, but they still understand spoken and written language. This condition occurs due to damage to Broca's area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the brain, often as a result of a stroke. Patients with Broca’s aphasia have difficulty forming complete sentences and may speak in short, broken phrases.

 

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Wernicke’s aphasia: In Wernicke’s aphasia, patients speak fluently but their speech is often nonsensical or irrelevant, and they have poor comprehension, which is not the case here.
 

Option C. Conduction aphasia: This type of aphasia involves an inability to repeat words or phrases, but speech remains fluent and comprehension is generally intact.
 

Option D. Global aphasia: This is the most severe form of aphasia, involving both speech production and comprehension difficulties, which does not match this patient’s presentation.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Broca’s aphasia presents as an inability to speak fluently, while comprehension remains intact, typically caused by damage to the inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Which muscle is attached to the marked bony structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Iliopsoas

 

The bony structure marked by the arrow is the lesser trochanter of the femur. The iliopsoas muscle, which is a combination of the iliacus and psoas major muscles, inserts on the lesser trochanter. This muscle plays a crucial role in hip flexion and is the strongest flexor of the thigh at the hip joint.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Gluteus maximus: This muscle inserts on the gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial tract, not the lesser trochanter.
 

Option C. Gluteus medius: This muscle inserts on the greater trochanter of the femur, not the lesser trochanter.
 

Option D. Sartorius: The sartorius inserts on the pes anserinus, which is on the medial surface of the tibia, not the femur.

 

Educational objectives:


The iliopsoas muscle inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur, making it the primary muscle responsible for hip flexion.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: In the given image, the tendon marked by the arrow is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Flexor carpi radialis

 

 

The flexor carpi radialis (FCR) tendon is located on the radial side of the forearm. It is responsible for flexing and abducting the wrist. In the image, the arrow marks the position of the FCR tendon, which lies lateral to the palmaris longus tendon (if present) and is easily palpable during wrist flexion.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Flexor carpi ulnaris: This tendon is located on the ulnar (pinky) side of the forearm and does not correspond to the marked position in the image.
 

Option C. Flexor digitorum superficialis: This tendon lies deeper and is not as easily palpable as the FCR.
 

Option D. Palmaris longus: This tendon, if present, would be positioned more medially compared to the flexor carpi radialis.

 

Educational objectives:


The flexor carpi radialis is a prominent tendon located on the radial side of the wrist and is marked in the image.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the muscle forming the marked boundary.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Extensor Pollicis Longus

 

 

The image points to the anatomical snuffbox, a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist. The boundaries of this snuffbox are formed by the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus (posteriorly), and the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis (anteriorly). The marked muscle in this image corresponds to the extensor pollicis longus, which forms the posterior boundary of the anatomical snuffbox.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Extensor Pollicis Brevis: This muscle forms the anterior boundary of the snuffbox but is not the marked muscle in this image.
 

Option B. Abductor Pollicis Longus: This muscle also forms part of the anterior boundary of the snuffbox but is not the correct answer.
 

Option C. Abductor Pollicis Brevis: This muscle is not part of the anatomical snuffbox and does not form any boundary.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The extensor pollicis longus forms the posterior boundary of the anatomical snuffbox and is the correct identification for the marked muscle in the image.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A young man came to the medical OPD with complaints of early morning backache and stiffness, which improves on exercise, and persistent red eyes. On examination, lung expansion was less than 3 cm. X-ray is shown in the image given below. What is the most probable diagnosis & which type of joint is involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ankylosing spondylitis & secondary cartilagenous joint

 

 

This patient presents with hallmark signs of Ankylosing spondylitis, including early morning backache that improves with exercise, persistent red eyes (suggestive of uveitis), and reduced lung expansion. Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints. The stiffness and decreased lung expansion occur due to inflammation of the spinal joints and costovertebral joints, which are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses), where the vertebrae are joined by fibrocartilage.

 

The X-ray image shows a "bamboo spine," which is a classic radiological finding in ankylosing spondylitis. This appearance results from the fusion of the vertebral bodies due to chronic inflammation. The involvement of secondary cartilaginous joints is central to the progression of the disease.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Ankylosing spondylitis & primary cartilagenous joint: This is incorrect because ankylosing spondylitis involves secondary cartilaginous joints (such as the spine and sacroiliac joints), 

 

Option C. Osteopetrosis & primary cartilagenous joint: Osteopetrosis is a condition characterized by abnormal bone density due to impaired osteoclast activity. It does not present with symptoms such as morning stiffness, back pain, or uveitis. It also does not primarily involve cartilaginous joints.

 

Option D. Osteopetrosis & secondary cartilagenous joint: Osteopetrosis does not affect secondary cartilaginous joints, 

 

Educational objective:
 

Ankylosing spondylitis involves secondary cartilaginous joints, especially the spine and sacroiliac joints, leading to stiffness, back pain, and reduced lung expansion. The "bamboo spine" appearance on X-ray is a characteristic feature

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman presents with a progressive decline in daily activity. She gives a history of convulsions and visual hallucinations. She does not talk to anyone and keeps looking at the sky. Pathological examination shows the presence of Lewy bodies within the neurons. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Parkinson's disease: 

 

The presence of Lewy bodies in the neurons is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease. This condition is a neurodegenerative disorder that primarily affects movement but can also cause non-motor symptoms such as cognitive decline, convulsions, and visual hallucinations, The patient's lack of interaction and fixation on the sky are also common in the later stages of Parkinson's disease.

 

Lewy bodies are abnormal aggregates of protein that develop inside nerve cells, contributing to the death of neurons and leading to the characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's, such as motor dysfunction and cognitive impairments. While Lewy bodies are found in other diseases, such as Lewy body dementia,

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Prion disease: Prion diseases, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, are caused by misfolded proteins and typically present with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and ataxia. They do not involve Lewy bodies 

 

Option C. Huntington's chorea: Huntington’s disease is a genetic disorder that leads to movement abnormalities, but it does not involve Lewy bodies. Its typical features include chorea (involuntary movements) and psychiatric symptoms, not the convulsions and visual hallucinations described here.

 

Option D. Alzheimer's disease: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, not Lewy bodies. While cognitive decline is common in Alzheimer's, the presence of Lewy bodies and the other symptoms point more towards Parkinson's disease 

 

Educational objective:
 

The presence of Lewy bodies in neurons is a key pathological finding in Parkinson’s disease, especially when combined with symptoms such as motor dysfunction, cognitive decline, and visual hallucinations.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old chronic smoker came to the medicine outpatient department with complaints of upper chest discomfort and drooping of an eyelid. He also complained of pain radiating to the upper arm and a tingling sensation in the 4th and 5th digits of his left hand. The chest X-ray is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Pancoast tumor


The patient's presentation, including upper chest discomfort, drooping of an eyelid, and pain radiating to the upper arm with tingling sensation in the 4th and 5th digits of the left hand, is characteristic of a Pancoast tumor. This type of tumor occurs at the apex of the lung and can compress nearby structures such as the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain, leading to symptoms like shoulder pain, arm tingling (especially along the distribution of the ulnar nerve), and Horner's syndrome (which includes ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis).

 

The X-ray shows a mass at the apex of the lung, consistent with a Pancoast tumor, which is typically associated with smoking and tends to invade surrounding tissues, causing these neurological symptoms.

 

Other Options:
 

Option B. Upper lobe pneumonia: While pneumonia in the upper lobe can cause chest discomfort and respiratory symptoms, it does not explain the neurological symptoms like drooping of the eyelid or arm tingling.

 

Option C. Superior vena cava obstruction: Superior vena cava obstruction usually presents with swelling of the face, neck, and upper limbs due to impaired venous return, rather than the neurological symptoms described in this case.

 

Option D. Aspergilloma: Aspergillomas are fungal balls that form in pre-existing lung cavities, often leading to cough and hemoptysis, but they do not typically cause neurological symptoms such as drooping of the eyelid or arm pain.

 

Educational objective:


Pancoast tumors are located at the lung apex and can cause shoulder pain, arm tingling, and Horner’s syndrome due to compression of nearby nerves and structures. The patient's smoking history and the X-ray findings support this diagnosis.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with anterior knee pain that worsens with activities like running and jumping. On physical examination, there is tenderness and swelling over the front of the knee. Palpation reveals a small, round, bony prominence at the centre of the knee. The patient reports no recent trauma. You will put the involved bone in which of the following types?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Sesamoid


The bone involved in this case is the patella, which is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body. Sesamoid bones are seed-like bones found within tendons, and they serve to reduce friction and modify pressure. The patella, located in front of the knee joint, helps improve the efficiency of the quadriceps muscle during knee extension. The presence of anterior knee pain, particularly in a patient with a history of running or jumping, suggests overuse of the patellar tendon, leading to inflammation or irritation in the sesamoid bone.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Sphenoid: The sphenoid bone is located in the skull and has no involvement in knee function.

 

Option B. Hyoid: The hyoid bone is located in the neck and serves as a point of attachment for tongue and neck muscles. It is not involved in knee function.

 

Option C. Ethmoid: The ethmoid bone is part of the skull, involved in forming the nasal cavity, and has no relation to the knee or patella.

 

Educational objective:


The patella is a sesamoid bone, and it plays a crucial role in knee extension by increasing the leverage of the quadriceps tendon.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: All of the following muscles have dual nerve supply except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pronator teres


The pronator teres is primarily innervated by the median nerve and does not have dual nerve supply. The anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), a branch of the median nerve, is also involved in innervating parts of the forearm, but the pronator teres itself is innervated by the median nerve alone. 

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Subscapularis: This muscle has dual nerve supply from the upper and lower subscapular nerves (USN, LSN).
 

Option B. Pectoralis major: The pectoralis major muscle is supplied by both the medial and lateral pectoral nerves (MPN, LPN).
 

Option D. Flexor digitorum profundus: This muscle has dual innervation from the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), a branch of the median nerve, and the ulnar nerve (UN).

 

Educational objective:
 

the pronator teres has a single nerve supply (median nerve), whereas the other muscles listed have dual nerve innervation​

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 45-year-old office worker complains of persistent wrist pain and difficulty performing repetitive tasks on a computer keyboard. Physical examination reveals tenderness at the wrist joint and decreased range of motion, particularly during wrist flexion and extension. Radiographic evaluation shows evidence of degenerative changes in the joint space. Which of the following bones is not directly involved in the formation of the wrist joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ulna


The ulna is not directly involved in the formation of the wrist joint. The radiocarpal joint (wrist joint) is formed by the radius articulating with the proximal carpal bones such as the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetral. The ulna is separated from the wrist joint by a fibrocartilage disc known as the articular disc, which prevents it from participating directly in the joint.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Scaphoid: The scaphoid is one of the proximal carpal bones that articulates directly with the radius, making it an essential part of the wrist joint.

 

Option C. Radius: The radius is a key bone in the formation of the radiocarpal joint, where it articulates with carpal bones like the scaphoid and lunate.

 

Option D. Triquetral: The triquetral is part of the proximal row of carpal bones, and while it has indirect involvement with the radius through its connection to the lunate, it is still considered part of the wrist joint.

 

Educational objective:
 

The ulna does not directly participate in the wrist joint due to the presence of the articular disc, separating it from the carpal bones

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient presents to the orthopedic clinic with complaints of progressive weakness in his right hand. The patient reports difficulty in fine movements of the hand. The doctor performed a test over the patient, as shown in the image. Which of the following statements is true about the given image?

options.label: A
options.text: The median nerve of the right hand is injured.

options.label: B
options.text: There is weakness of thenar muscles on the right side.

options.label: C
options.text: The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak.

options.label: D
options.text: The flexor muscles of the thumb of the right hand are weak.

questions.answerText: The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak.


The test shown in the image is known as the "book test" or "Froment's sign". This test is used to assess the strength of the adductor pollicis muscle, which is innervated by the ulnar nerve. In this test, a piece of paper is placed between the thumb and the index finger, and the patient is asked to hold the paper while the examiner tries to pull it away. A positive Froment’s sign, as seen in the image, indicates that the patient compensates by flexing the thumb at the interphalangeal joint due to weakness of the adductor pollicis. This compensation is performed by the flexor pollicis longus, which is innervated by the median nerve. Thus, the ulnar nerve, specifically the branch supplying the adductor pollicis.

 

In the question it is mentioned that the patient is having difficulty in fine movement of the hand which is also the hint that there is injury to the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve is also known as musician's nerve and is responsible for fine movement since it supplies 15 out of 20 muscles in the hand. 

 

 

Other Options:


Option A. The median nerve of the right hand is injured: This option is incorrect because the median nerve would primarily affect the thenar muscles, leading to weakness in thumb opposition. However, the test performed is assessing the function of the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve.

 

Option B. There is weakness of thenar muscles on the right side: While weakness of the thenar muscles is associated with median nerve injury, this test focuses on the adductor pollicis, which is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

 

Option D. The flexor muscles of the thumb of the right hand are weak: The flexor muscles of the thumb, particularly the flexor pollicis longus, are not the focus of this test. In fact, patients with a positive Froment’s sign use the flexor pollicis longus (innervated by the median nerve) to compensate for the weakness of the adductor pollicis.

 

Educational objective:


The book test is used to evaluate the function of the adductor pollicis muscle, and a positive result indicates weakness in this muscle, commonly due to ulnar nerve injury

 

Ulnar nerve Tests (ABCDEFGH) 

 

A:- A/Ulnar nerve 

B:- Book test 

C:- Card test (positive in Palmar interossei damage) 

D:- aDDuctor pollicis test 

E:- Egawa test( positive in dorsal interossei damage) 

F:- Froment test 

G:- Guyon’s tunnel syndrome 

H:- Handlebar palsy 

 

Educational Objective:
 

The ulnar nerve is known as a musician's nerve and is responsible for the fine movement of the hand. The median nerve is known as labourers nerve.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked structure:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Accessory nerve

 

The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) is responsible for innervating the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. This nerve runs across the posterior triangle of the neck, it can be identified due to its position along the path associated with these muscles. The accessory nerve typically crosses the posterior triangle in an oblique direction, making it distinguishable in this region.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Transverse cervical nerve: This nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the anterior neck. It does not follow the same path as the accessory nerve and would be located in a different region of the neck.

 

Option B. Lesser occipital nerve: This nerve runs along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and innervates the skin of the neck and scalp behind the ear. Its location does not match the nerve marked in the image.

 

Option C. Great auricular nerve: This nerve supplies sensation to the skin over the parotid gland and the auricle. It typically ascends vertically along the sternocleidomastoid muscle, but its location does not correspond to the marked structure in the image.

 

Educational objective:

 

The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) runs through the posterior triangle of the neck, innervating the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old null gravida Caucasian patient presented with a 15-month history of amenorrhea, bifrontal headache, and photophobia. Examination revealed general physical, neurologic, and ophthalmoscopic findings with normal visual fields. A pelvic examination revealed normal external genitalia, nulliparous cervix and uterus, and bilateral cystic ovarian masses measuring 8 cm in diameter on the right and 4 cm on the left. Endocrine evaluation revealed an elevated serum prolactin in the range of 48 to 50 ng/ml. This situation was related with mass in the following area of the below image:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The patient’s elevated serum prolactin and bilateral cystic ovarian masses are indicative of a prolactinoma, a type of pituitary adenoma that causes hyperprolactinemia. this condition leads to menstrual disturbances such as amenorrhea, as seen in this patient. The mass responsible for the condition is located in the pituitary gland, which resides in the sella turcica (Turkish saddle), marked as area B in the image. The pituitary gland secretes prolactin, and a tumor in this region leads to excessive hormone secretion, 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A: This area represents the crista galli, a bony ridge in the anterior cranial fossa. It is not related to the pituitary gland or prolactin secretion.

 

Option C. C: This area corresponds to the internal acoustic meatus, which is involved in auditory and vestibular functions. It has no relation to pituitary adenomas or prolactin secretion.

 

Option D. D: This area marks the foramen magnum, which is the opening in the skull through which the spinal cord passes. It is not related to the pituitary gland or prolactinoma.

 

Educational objective:

 

A prolactinoma, located in the pituitary gland (in the sella turcica), can cause elevated serum prolactin levels, amenorrhea, and ovarian cysts.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old female patient presented with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, which is often accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals multiple peptic ulcers in the duodenal bulb. Laboratory tests show elevated gastrin levels. She was given Prilosec for a long time. She was also consuming a vegetarian diet and now presented with tiredness & palpitations since a month. She complained of progressive sensory loss in her lower extremities. Neurological examination reveals impaired vibratory sensation in both legs. An MRI of the spinal cord shows no structural abnormalities. On blood examination, the following hematological slide was found. All of the following statements are correct in this case except:

options.label: A
options.text: This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decreased Vitamin B12 absorption.

options.label: C
options.text: In this patient due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.

options.label: D
options.text: On hematological examination, increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found.

questions.answerText: In this patient due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) In this patient due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.

 

The patient’s condition is due to gastrinoma, which causes high levels of gastrin and leads to hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid, resulting in multiple peptic ulcers. The use of Prilosec, a proton pump inhibitor, over a long period can cause malabsorption of Vitamin B12, especially in a vegetarian diet, as this patient followed. A deficiency in Vitamin B12 is known to affect myelination in the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus), which are responsible for proprioception and vibratory sensations. In this case, vibratory sensation is impaired, pointing to involvement of the dorsal columns, not the anterior spinothalamic tract, which is responsible for pain and temperature sensation.

 

The hematological findings, such as increased MCV and hypersegmented neutrophils, are classic signs of megaloblastic anemia caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid: This statement is correct, as gastrinoma leads to elevated gastrin levels and results in excessive acid production, causing peptic ulcers.

 

Option B. Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decreased Vitamin B12 absorption: This statement is correct, as prolonged use of proton pump inhibitors such as Prilosec can interfere with Vitamin B12 absorption.

 

Option D. On haematological examination, increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found: This is also correct, as these findings are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia, which is commonly caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

Educational objective:

 

Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to myelination defects primarily in the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus), not the anterior spinothalamic tract.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: SSA fibres are present in which of the following cranial nerves?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) I, II, VIII

 

SSA (Special Somatic Afferent) fibers are present in cranial nerves I, II, and VIII. These fibers are involved in special senses like vision, hearing, and balance. Cranial nerve I (olfactory) is responsible for smell, cranial nerve II (optic) is responsible for vision, and cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear) is responsible for hearing and balance. SSA fibers do not exist in cranial nerve VII, which is primarily involved in facial expression and taste.

 

Note - Cranial nerve VII (facial) does not contain SSA fibers. It is involved in motor function and the sense of taste but not in vision, hearing, or balance.

 

Educational objective:

 

SSA fibers are found in cranial nerves I, II, and VIII, which are involved in special senses like vision, hearing, and balance.

questions.stem: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 6th arch

 

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery. During embryological development, the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the 6th arch artery on the left side. The ligamentum arteriosum, which is a remnant of the 6th arch, helps maintain this configuration. On the right side, the corresponding artery disappears, which explains why the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery instead. Therefore, the 6th arch artery is crucial in forming the pathway for the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 3rd arch: The 3rd arch artery contributes to the formation of the common carotid and part of the internal carotid artery, not related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option B. 4th arch: The 4th arch artery gives rise to parts of the aorta and subclavian artery, but it is not directly responsible for the pathway of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option C. 5th arch: The 5th arch is either absent or rudimentary in human development, playing no role in the pathway of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Educational objective:

 

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the 6th arch artery, which plays a key role in its embryological development.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male patient presents with midline swelling in the neck. The swelling moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thyroglossal cyst

 

The most likely diagnosis is a thyroglossal cyst. Swellings located in the midline of the neck, which move with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue, are typically related to the thyroglossal duct. The thyroid gland is connected to the base of the tongue through this duct, and any remnants can lead to the formation of a thyroglossal cyst. The cyst’s movement with swallowing and tongue protrusion is a hallmark feature.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Brachial cyst: Brachial cysts are usually found lateral to the midline, most commonly in the anterior triangle of the neck, and do not move with deglutition or tongue protrusion.

 

Option C. Plunging ranula: A plunging ranula originates from the floor of the mouth and extends into the neck. It is not typically a midline structure, nor does it move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.

 

Option D. Dermoid cyst: Dermoid cysts can occur in the midline but generally do not move with deglutition or tongue protrusion, making them less likely than a thyroglossal cyst in this case.

 

Educational objective:

 

A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion due to its connection with the thyroglossal duct.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old male patient presents with a swelling that has been slowly growing in the past 2 years. On examination, it was variable in consistency and fully mobile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Parotid tumor

 

The most likely diagnosis is parotid tumor, particularly pleomorphic adenoma. a slowly growing mass, variable in consistency, and fully mobile is characteristic of a parotid tumor. It mentions that this tumor is encapsulated by the parotid fascia, making it mobile. The pleomorphic adenoma is a common benign tumor of the parotid gland, and its slow growth aligns with the patient’s symptoms of a two-year history of gradual enlargement.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dermoid cyst: Dermoid cysts are typically found in the midline and do not generally grow in the area described for this case. They also do not fit the description of a swelling with variable consistency and mobility.

 

Option C. Sebaceous cyst: Sebaceous cysts are usually smaller, often have a visible punctum, and do not grow as slowly or present with such variable consistency.

 

Option D. Cervical lymph node: Enlarged cervical lymph nodes tend to be firmer and less mobile than a benign parotid tumor. They often grow due to infection or malignancy and do not exhibit the slow, variable growth seen here.

 

Educational objective:

 

A parotid tumor, specifically pleomorphic adenoma, typically presents as a slow-growing, mobile, and variably consistent mass.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: The movements at the _________________ joint permit a person to look to the right and left.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Atlanto-axial

 

The atlanto-axial joint allows for the rotation of the head, which enables a person to look to the right and left. This joint is formed between the first and second cervical vertebrae (C1 and C2). The atlas (C1) rotates around the dens of the axis (C2), allowing for head rotation. This movement is distinct from the atlanto-occipital joint, which is responsible for the nodding motion 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Atlanto-occipital: This joint is responsible for the nodding "yes" movement and does not permit the rotational movement needed to look left or right.

 

Option C. C2-C3: This joint contributes to general neck movements but does not play a key role in the specific rotation of the head, which is primarily controlled by the atlanto-axial joint.

 

Option D. C3-C4: Like the C2-C3 joint, this joint is involved in neck flexion and extension but does not allow the significant rotational movement controlled by the atlanto-axial joint.

 

Educational objective:

 

The atlanto-axial joint is responsible for allowing rotational movements of the head, enabling a person to look left and right.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Shown epithelium is found in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Urinary bladder

 

 

The epithelium shown in the image is transitional epithelium, also known as urothelium. This type of epithelium is found in the urinary bladder. It has a unique structure that allows it to stretch, which is essential for accommodating fluctuations in the volume of urine. The cells are arranged in layers, and the superficial layer consists of large, dome-shaped cells known as "umbrella cells." These cells flatten when the bladder is distended and return to their dome shape when the bladder is empty, allowing the bladder to expand and contract without damaging the tissue.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Stomach: The stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium, not transitional epithelium. This tissue type does not accommodate stretching like the epithelium in the bladder.

 

Option B. Lungs: The lungs are lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium in the bronchi, and simple squamous epithelium in the alveoli, neither of which resemble the transitional epithelium seen in the bladder.

 

Option C. Liver: The liver is composed of hepatocytes and is not lined by any epithelium resembling that in the image. Its structure is vastly different from transitional epithelium.

 

Educational objective:

 

Transitional epithelium, or urothelium, is found in the urinary bladder and allows for stretching to accommodate urine volume changes.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of cartilage shown in the image below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Elastic cartilage


The image illustrates elastic cartilage, which is distinct due to the presence of a dense network of elastic fibers embedded in the cartilage matrix. Elastic cartilage has the following key characteristics:

It contains chondrocytes (cartilage cells) located within lacunae, similar to other types of cartilage, but it is distinguished by the elastic fibers that surround the chondrocytes.

 

The elastic fibers are visible in the extracellular matrix, providing flexibility and the ability to return to its original shape after deformation.

Elastic cartilage is commonly found in areas of the body where flexible support is required, such as the external ear (auricle), the epiglottis, and certain parts of the larynx. It allows these structures to bend and then resume their shape.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Hyaline cartilage: Hyaline cartilage is the most common type of cartilage. It has a glassy and smooth appearance under a microscope because it lacks visible fibers in the matrix. It is found in the joints (articular cartilage), trachea, nose, and costal cartilage. The absence of prominent fibers in hyaline cartilage distinguishes it from elastic cartilage.

 

Option C. Articular cartilage: This is a specialized form of hyaline cartilage, found at the ends of long bones in synovial joints, providing a smooth surface for movement. While it shares the glassy appearance of hyaline cartilage, it lacks the elastic fibers that define elastic cartilage. Articular cartilage has excellent resistance to wear but lacks flexibility compared to elastic cartilage.

 

Option D. Fibrocartilage: Fibrocartilage is very different in appearance from both hyaline and elastic cartilage. It contains thick bundles of collagen fibers, giving it a dense, fibrous texture under the microscope. It is found in regions that require tough, supportive structures, such as the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, and menisci of the knee. The absence of elastic fibers and the presence of collagen bundles set fibrocartilage apart from elastic cartilage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

 

(Mnemonic - ETC NEWS) 

 

E - Ear pinna 

E - Eustachian tube 

E - Epiglottis 

T - Tip of nose 

T - Tip of arytenoid cartilage 

T - Tritiate cartilage 

C - Corniculate 

C - Cuneiform

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Purkinje cells

 

The cell marked in the histological image is a Purkinje cell. Purkinje cells are flask-shaped neurons located in the Purkinje layer of the cerebellum. These cells have a large, prominent nucleus and are responsible for transmitting signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei. The Purkinje cell layer is situated between the molecular layer above and the granular layer below. The distinctive flask-shaped structure of these cells makes them easy to identify. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Basket cells: These are found in the molecular layer and are inhibitory interneurons that form synapses with Purkinje cells, but they are not large or flask-shaped like the marked cell in the image.

 

Option C. Golgi cells: These cells are located in the granular layer, below the Purkinje layer, and serve an inhibitory role on granule cells. However, they are smaller and not flask-shaped like Purkinje cells.

 

Option D. Granule cells: Granule cells are small neurons found in the granular layer, far smaller than Purkinje cells, and do not have the large flask-shaped appearance seen in the image.

 

Educational objective:

 

Purkinje cells are large, flask-shaped neurons located in the Purkinje layer of the cerebellum and are essential for coordinating motor activity.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: When capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures are 3 mm of Hg and 0 mm of Hg and colloid oncotic pressure of capillaries and interstitium is 25 mm of Hg and 5 mm of Hg, What is the Net filtration pressure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 17 mm Hg

 

The Net Filtration Pressure (NFP) is calculated using the formula:

 

NFP=(Capillary Hydrostatic Pressure− Capillary Oncotic Pressure)-(Interstitial Hydrostatic Pressure −Interstitial Oncotic Pressure)

 

Given values:

 

  • Capillary Hydrostatic Pressure (HPc) = 3 mmHg
  • Interstitial Hydrostatic Pressure (HPi) = 0 mmHg
  • Capillary Oncotic Pressure (OPc) = 25 mmHg
  • Interstitial Oncotic Pressure (OPi) = 5 mmHg

 

NFP = (3−25)−(0−5)

 

NFP = -22+5

 

NFP = −17 mmHg

 

The negative value (-17 mmHg) indicates that the fluid is moving into the capillaries (reabsorption occurs rather than filtration). Since the answer choices do not include negative values, we take the absolute value:

 

Net Reabsorption Pressure=17 mmHg

 

Educational Objective:

 

Net Filtration Pressure (NFP) is calculated as the difference between hydrostatic and oncotic pressures in capillaries and interstitium. A negative NFP means net reabsorption into capillaries, preventing edema. ​​

questions.stem: In a given arteriolar blood vessel, the pressure is held constant and the radius is decreased. The resultant change in blood flow could also be accomplished by keeping pressure and radius constant and changing which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Increasing viscosity

 

To determine how blood flow changes with radius and other factors, we use Poiseuille’s Law, which describes laminar flow in a vessel:

 

 

Where:

 

  • Q = Blood Flow
  • ΔP = Pressure Difference
  • r = Radius of the Vessel
  • η = Blood Viscosity
  • L = Length of the Vessel

 

Step-by-Step Analysis:

 

1st Scenario: Decreasing Radius (Given Condition)

 

  • Radius (r) is reduced, so blood flow decreases significantly (since r⁴ is in the numerator).

 

2nd Scenario: Achieving the Same Result Without Changing Radius or Pressure

 

  • Since radius (r) and pressure (ΔP) must remain constant, we must reduce blood flow (Q) by modifying other variables.
  • According to Poiseuille’s Law, flow is inversely proportional to viscosity (η) and length (L).
  • Increasing viscosity (η) would decrease blood flow, just as decreasing the radius would have done.

 

Thus, the correct answer is D. Increasing viscosity, as it achieves the same reduction in blood flow without altering radius or pressure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreasing compliance: Incorrect.

 

  • Compliance refers to how easily a vessel expands with pressure.
  • It does not directly affect resistance or flow in this scenario.

 

Option B. Decreasing flow path length: Incorrect.

 

  • Shortening vessel length (L) would increase blood flow, opposite to the expected result.
  • To decrease flow, length should increase, not decrease.

 

Option C. Decreasing resistance: Incorrect. Resistance (R) is inversely proportional to flow, so decreasing resistance would increase flow, not decrease it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Poiseuille’s Law states that blood flow (Q) is directly proportional to the fourth power of the vessel radius and inversely proportional to viscosity and vessel length. To decrease flow without changing radius or pressure, increasing viscosity (η) is the best option.
