questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: MMC (migrating motor complexes) occurs at the rate of ___ and at an interval of_________:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 5 cm/min, 90 min 

 

Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is a cyclic pattern of electrical and mechanical activity observed in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract during fasting. MMC is responsible for clearing residual food particles, secretions, and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine in between meals.

 

Key Characteristics of MMC:

 

  1. Occurs every 90 minutes during fasting.
  2. Moves at a speed of ~5 cm/min through the small intestine.
  3. Triggered by motilin, a hormone released cyclically during fasting.
  4. Divided into four phases (I-IV), with phase III being the strongest contraction phase.

 

Since MMC occurs at an interval of 90 minutes and moves at a rate of 5 cm/min, the correct answer is B (5 cm/min, 90 min).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) occurs in fasting states at intervals of 90 minutes and moves at a rate of approximately 5 cm/min, helping clear the gastrointestinal tract between meals.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following accurately describes the cardiovascular regulation?

options.label: A
options.text: Baroreceptors get activated in hypotension and help increase Blood pressure

options.label: B
options.text: Baroreceptors inhibit the nucleus ambiguous which inhibits the sympathetic system

options.label: C
options.text: Nucleus tractus solitarius activates vagal centres

options.label: D
options.text: Vagus nerve carries afferent fibres from carotid sinus baroreceptors

questions.answerText: Nucleus tractus solitarius activates vagal centres
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Nucleus tractus solitarius activates vagal centres

 

The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) plays a crucial role in cardiovascular regulation by receiving afferent signals from baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. When blood pressure increases, NTS activates vagal centers, particularly the nucleus ambiguus, which increases parasympathetic (vagal) activity to slow the heart rate and lower blood pressure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Baroreceptors get activated in hypotension and help increase blood pressure:

 

  • Baroreceptors are activated in hypertension, not hypotension.
  • In hypotension, baroreceptor firing decreases, leading to increased sympathetic activity to raise BP.

 

Option B. Baroreceptors inhibit the nucleus ambiguus, which inhibits the sympathetic system: 

 

  • The nucleus ambiguus is a parasympathetic center that reduces heart rate.
  • Baroreceptors activate (not inhibit) the nucleus ambiguus.

 

Option D. Vagus nerve carries afferent fibers from carotid sinus baroreceptors: 

 

  • The carotid sinus baroreceptors send afferent signals via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the vagus nerve (CN X).
  • The vagus nerve (CN X) carries afferent fibers from the aortic arch baroreceptors, not the carotid sinus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) plays a central role in cardiovascular regulation by receiving baroreceptor signals and activating vagal centers to reduce blood pressure. Baroreceptors respond to increased BP, not hypotension, and send afferent signals via CN IX (carotid sinus) and CN X (aortic arch).

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the sleep wave marked in the EEG during sleep wake cycle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) REM Sleep

 

The EEG image shows high-frequency, low-amplitude waves, which are characteristic of REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep.

 

  • REM sleep is also called paradoxical sleep because, despite the deep sleep state, brain activity resembles wakefulness.
  • The beta waves seen in the image (high frequency, low amplitude) are typically associated with an awake state, but they also appear in REM sleep.
  • During REM sleep:
    • EEG shows beta waves (similar to wakefulness).
    • Electromyogram (EMG) shows muscle atonia (paralysis below the neck, preventing movement during dreams).
    • Electro-oculogram (EOG) shows rapid eye movements (hence the name REM sleep).
    • Memory consolidation occurs, and dreams are vividly remembered.

 

Thus, the marked EEG wave corresponds to REM sleep 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. NREM Stage 1: NREM Stage 1 shows theta waves (low amplitude, moderate frequency), but the given EEG has high-frequency beta waves.

 

Option B. NREM Stage 2: NREM Stage 2 is characterized by sleep spindles and K-complexes, neither of which are present in the given EEG.

 

Option C. NREM Stage 3: NREM Stage 3 (deep sleep) is dominated by delta waves (low frequency, high amplitude), which are not seen in the given EEG.

 

Educational Objective:

 

REM sleep, also known as paradoxical sleep, is characterized by beta waves on EEG, rapid eye movements (seen on EOG), and muscle atonia (seen on EMG). It is essential for memory consolidation and is the phase where vivid dreaming occurs.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A young man met with a motor bike accident and had injury to ileum and jejunum. Therefore the entire ileum and partial jejunum was resected. Which of the following would the patient suffer from?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Vitamin B12 deficiency

 

The ileum and jejunum play crucial roles in the absorption of essential nutrients. Since the entire ileum and part of the jejunum were resected, the patient will suffer from deficiencies related to these regions, particularly Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

  • Vitamin B12 absorption occurs in the terminal ileum, where it binds to intrinsic factor (produced by gastric parietal cells).
  • Intrinsic factor escorts Vitamin B12 from the stomach until it reaches the ileum, where it is absorbed.
  • If the ileum is removed, Vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed, leading to pernicious anemia and neurological deficits.

 

Thus, the most likely consequence of ileal resection is Vitamin B12 deficiency

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Constipation:

 

  • The opposite effect (diarrhea) is more likely because the ileum is responsible for bile acid reabsorption.
  • Resection of the ileum causes bile acid malabsorption, leading to secretory diarrhea rather than constipation.

 

Option C. Gastric ulcer:

 

  • Gastric ulcers are primarily caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use, not by resection of the ileum and jejunum.
  • There is no direct link between small intestine resection and gastric ulcers.

 

Option D. Diarrhea:

 

  • While diarrhea can occur due to bile acid malabsorption, the most significant deficiency due to ileal resection is Vitamin B12.
  • Since the question asks for the most prominent issue, Vitamin B12 deficiency is a more direct consequence.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The terminal ileum is the primary site for Vitamin B12 and bile acid absorption. Resection of the ileum leads to Vitamin B12 deficiency, which can cause pernicious anemia and neurological symptoms.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Detachment of myosin head from actin is caused by:

options.label: B
options.text: Attachment of ATP to the head

options.label: C
options.text: Binding of ADP and Pi to the head

questions.answerText: Attachment of ATP to the head
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Attachment of ATP to the head

 

Detachment of the myosin head from actin occurs due to the binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head. This is a crucial step in the cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction.

 

  1. ATP binding to myosin causes detachment from actin
    • ATP binds to myosin, leading to the release of myosin from actin, thereby causing muscle relaxation.
  2. ATP hydrolysis activates myosin
    • Once myosin detaches, ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP and Pi by myosin ATPase, energizing the myosin head.
  3. Power stroke occurs when Pi is released
    • The removal of inorganic phosphate (Pi) provides the energy for the power stroke, allowing myosin to pull the actin filament inward.

 

Thus, ATP attachment causes relaxation (detachment from actin), while Pi release provides energy for contraction.

 

Since attachment of ATP is required for detachment of myosin from actin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Change in troponin C configuration:

 

  • Troponin C regulates tropomyosin movement by binding Ca²⁺, which exposes the actin binding site.
  • However, it does not cause myosin to detach from actin.

 

Option C. Binding of ADP and Pi to the head:

 

  • Binding of ADP and Pi keeps myosin in an activated state, ready for attachment to actin.
  • Detachment only occurs when ATP binds, not ADP/Pi.

 

Option D. Pumping Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum:

 

  • Ca²⁺ reuptake (via SERCA pump) helps terminate contraction but does not directly cause myosin detachment.
  • ATP binding is required for detachment, not just Ca²⁺ removal.

 

Educational Objective:

 

ATP binding to myosin causes its detachment from actin, leading to muscle relaxation. ATP hydrolysis re-energizes myosin, and the release of Pi provides energy for the power stroke during contraction.

questions.stem: Correct sequence after ‘a' wave of JVP- Rapid ejectionR wave 1st Heart SoundT wave in ECG Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2 → 3 → 1 → 4

 

The ‘a’ wave in the Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) represents atrial contraction (atrial systole). After this, the sequence of cardiac events follows a logical electrical → mechanical progression, as electrical depolarization occurs first and then leads to mechanical contraction.

 

The correct sequence after the ‘a’ wave is:

 

2. R wave (QRS complex in ECG)

 

  • The R wave corresponds to ventricular depolarization, signaling the start of ventricular systole.
  • Electrical events always precede mechanical contraction.

 

3. First Heart Sound (S1)

 

  • The first heart sound (S1) occurs when the atrioventricular (AV) valves (mitral and tricuspid) close due to ventricular contraction.
  • This marks the beginning of isovolumetric contraction.

 

1. Rapid Ejection Phase

 

  • After isovolumetric contraction, once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic and pulmonary valves open, leading to the rapid ejection phase of systole.

 

4. T wave in ECG

 

  • The T wave represents ventricular repolarization, initiating ventricular relaxation (diastole).
  • The slow ejection phase follows rapid ejection, but T wave occurs near the transition from rapid to slow ejection.

 

Thus, the correct order is:


R wave (2) → First heart sound (3) → Rapid ejection (1) → T wave (4).

 

This matches Option C (2 → 3 → 1 → 4).

 

Educational Objective:

 

After the ‘a’ wave (atrial contraction), the sequence of cardiac events follows: R wave (ventricular depolarization) → S1 (AV valve closure) → Rapid ejection → T wave (ventricular repolarization). Electrical events precede mechanical events.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic for a routine check-up. His medications include an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic which can affect the tubulo-glomerular feedback. Which one of the following is primarily regulated by the tubulo-glomerular feedback mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) GFR

 

Tubuloglomerular Feedback (TGF) is a key mechanism involved in the autoregulation of Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).

 

  • It functions through the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), which monitors sodium chloride (NaCl) levels in the distal tubule via macula densa cells.
  • If GFR increases, more NaCl reaches the macula densa, leading to adenosine release, which causes afferent arteriole vasoconstriction → reducing GFR back to normal.
  • If GFR decreases, renin is released, leading to angiotensin II production → causing efferent arteriole constriction to restore GFR.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Plasma Sodium:

 

  • TGF monitors NaCl levels, but its primary function is to adjust GFR, not regulate systemic sodium concentration.
  • Sodium balance is mainly controlled by aldosterone and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

 

Option C. Plasma Volume:

 

  • Plasma volume is primarily regulated by RAAS and ADH (antidiuretic hormone), not by tubuloglomerular feedback.
  • While TGF plays a role in adjusting GFR, it does not directly regulate plasma volume.

 

Option D. Determining Tubular Secretion:

 

  • TGF does not regulate tubular secretion; it only adjusts GFR based on NaCl levels.
  • Tubular secretion is mainly controlled by hormonal and transport mechanisms in the nephron.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) is an autoregulatory mechanism that primarily regulates GFR by adjusting afferent and efferent arteriole resistance in response to NaCl concentration changes at the macula densa.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: In 50-year-old patient with respiratory distress, FEV1 = 1.5litre and FVC =3.0 litres. The type of disease he is suffering from:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bronchitis

 

The FEV1/FVC ratio is a key parameter used to differentiate between obstructive and restrictive lung diseases.

 

  • FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second) = 1.5 L
  • FVC (Forced Vital Capacity) = 3.0 L
  • FEV1/FVC ratio = (1.5/3.0) × 100 = 50%

 

Interpreting FEV1/FVC Ratio:

 

  • Normal FEV1/FVC ratio: ≥ 80%
  • Obstructive Lung Disease: < 70%
  • Restrictive Lung Disease: ≥ 80% with decreased FVC

 

Since the patient's FEV1/FVC ratio is 50% (which is low), this indicates an obstructive lung disease. Bronchitis is an example of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which fits this pattern.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fibrosis:

 

  • Pulmonary fibrosis is a restrictive lung disease, where FEV1/FVC ratio is usually normal or increased (≥80%).
  • The given patient has a reduced ratio, which is typical of obstructive lung disease, not fibrosis.

 

Option C. Tuberculosis:

 

  • Tuberculosis can cause fibrosis, leading to restrictive lung disease.
  • Like fibrosis, restrictive lung diseases have normal or high FEV1/FVC ratios.

 

Option D. Both A and C:

 

  • Since both fibrosis and tuberculosis are restrictive lung diseases, and this patient has an obstructive pattern, this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (<70%) is a hallmark of obstructive lung diseases like bronchitis, whereas restrictive lung diseases (e.g., fibrosis, tuberculosis) show a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio (≥80%).

questions.stem: If a substances appears in the renal artery but not in the renal vein:

options.label: A
options.text: Its clearance is equal to the glomerular filtration rate.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be reabsorbed by the kidney

options.label: C
options.text: Its urinary concentration must be higher than its plasma concentration

options.label: D
options.text: Its clearance is equal to the renal plasma flow

questions.answerText: Its clearance is equal to the renal plasma flow
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Its clearance is equal to the renal plasma flow

 

If a substance appears in the renal artery but not in the renal vein, this means that the kidney has completely removed it from circulation. This implies that:

 

  1. All of the substance was either filtered, secreted, or both in the nephron.
  2. None of the substance returned to the bloodstream via the renal vein (i.e., it was not reabsorbed).
  3. Such a substance must have a clearance equal to the renal plasma flow (RPF) because every molecule that entered the kidney was excreted.

 

The classic example of such a substance is Para-Aminohippuric Acid (PAH), which is both filtered and actively secreted in the tubules, making its clearance a close estimate of renal plasma flow (RPF). 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Its clearance is equal to the glomerular filtration rate:

 

  • If a substance's clearance equals the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), it means it is only filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted (e.g., inulin or creatinine).
  • However, in this case, the substance is entirely removed from circulation, meaning it must also be secreted, making its clearance equal to RPF, not just GFR.

 

Option B. It must be reabsorbed by the kidney:

 

  • If a substance were reabsorbed, it would partially return to the renal vein, meaning it would still be present in the renal venous blood.
  • Since the question states that the substance does not appear in the renal vein, it cannot be reabsorbed.

 

Option C. Its urinary concentration must be higher than its plasma concentration:

 

  • While the urinary concentration is often higher for secreted substances, this does not necessarily mean that the substance is completely removed from the bloodstream.
  • Some substances may have a high urine concentration but still be present in the renal vein.
  • The defining feature here is complete clearance, which relates to renal plasma flow, not just urine concentration.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A substance that appears in the renal artery but not in the renal vein must be completely excreted by the kidney, meaning its clearance equals the renal plasma flow (RPF). Para-Aminohippuric Acid (PAH) is the classic example of such a substance.

questions.stem: All are true about Decerebrate posture except:

options.label: A
options.text: Extension of both upper and lower extremity

options.label: B
options.text: Flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity

options.label: D
options.text: Reticulo spinal tract is also involved.

questions.answerText: Flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity 

 

Decerebrate posture is characterized by extension of both the upper and lower extremities due to loss of inhibitory control from higher brain centers.

 

  1. Cause of Decerebrate Posture:
    • It occurs due to a lesion at or below the red nucleus (midbrain, between the superior and inferior colliculi).
    • Disruption of the rubrospinal tract leads to loss of flexor control, causing unopposed extensor activity mediated by the reticulospinal tract.
  2. Key Features of Decerebrate Posture:
    • Both upper and lower limbs are extended (due to dominant pontine reticulospinal and vestibulospinal tracts).
    • Gamma motor neurons are hyperactive, leading to increased extensor tone.
    • Reticulospinal tract is involved, specifically the pontine reticulospinal tract, which enhances extensor tone.

 

Since decerebrate posture involves extension of both upper and lower limbs, option B (flexion of upper extremity and extension of lower extremity) is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extension of both upper and lower extremity: This is the hallmark feature of decerebrate posture due to loss of flexor control (rubrospinal tract) and dominance of extensor pathways (reticulospinal tract).

 

Option C. Exaggerated gamma motor neuron discharge:

 

  • Gamma motor neurons are hyperactive, leading to increased muscle tone and rigidity in both upper and lower limbs.
  • This contributes to the extensor hypertonia seen in decerebrate posture.

 

Option D. Reticulospinal tract is also involved:

 

  • Pontine reticulospinal tract is dominant in decerebrate posture, facilitating extensor tone.
  • The medullary reticulospinal tract (which normally inhibits extensors) is suppressed, allowing increased extensor activity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Decerebrate posture is characterized by extension of both upper and lower extremities due to brainstem damage below the red nucleus, leading to loss of rubrospinal tract function and dominance of the pontine reticulospinal tract.

questions.stemHtml: The graph below represents the relationship of chest, lung and both together w.r.t. the transmural pressure:

options.label: A
options.text: A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Residual Volume

options.label: B
options.text: A= Curve for Lung; B= Curve for Chest wall; X= Residual Volume

options.label: C
options.text: A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Functional Residual Capacity

options.label: D
options.text: A= Curve for Lung; B= Curve for Chest wall; X= Functional Residual Capacity

questions.answerText: A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Functional Residual Capacity
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) A= Curve for chest wall; B= Curve for Lung; X= Functional Residual Capacity

 

The given graph illustrates the relationship between chest wall compliance, lung compliance, and total lung capacity with transmural pressure.

 

  1. Curve A represents the chest wall:
    • The chest wall has a natural tendency to expand outward due to its elastic recoil.
    • At negative transmural pressures, it tries to expand.
    • This curve starts in the negative transmural pressure zone and moves towards equilibrium.
  2. Curve B represents the lung:
    • The lung has a natural tendency to collapse inward due to its elastic recoil.
    • At zero transmural pressure, it remains collapsed.
    • This curve starts in the positive transmural pressure zone, indicating the lung is always under positive pressure to prevent collapse.
  3. Integrated Curve (Blue Line):
    • This represents the combined effect of chest wall and lung compliance in balancing each other.
    • The equilibrium point (X) where both forces equalize is the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), which is the lung volume after normal expiration when no respiratory muscles are actively contracting.

 

Thus, option C is correct, where:

 

  • A = Chest Wall Curve
  • B = Lung Curve
  • X = Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)

 

Educational Objective:

 

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the lung volume at which the inward elastic recoil of the lung is balanced by the outward recoil of the chest wall, creating a state of equilibrium with no active muscular effort.

questions.stemHtml: The following diagram shows the depth of respiration of a 45-year-old man who suffered a head injury in an automobile accident. This “crescendodecrescendo” pattern of breathing is called which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Cheyne-Stokes breathing

 

The given graph represents a crescendo-decrescendo pattern of breathing, which is characteristic of Cheyne-Stokes respiration (CSR).

 

  1. Cheyne-Stokes Breathing Pattern:
    • It is defined by gradual hyperventilation (crescendo) followed by a gradual hypoventilation (decrescendo) and then apnea.
    • This cycle repeats, causing a waxing and waning pattern of breathing.
    • Commonly associated with high altitude, heart failure, and brain injuries (e.g., head trauma, stroke, brainstem lesions).
  2. Mechanism of Cheyne-Stokes Breathing:
    • Hypoxia and fluctuating CO₂ levels play a major role in CSR.
    • Initially, hypoxia and hypercapnia stimulate hyperventilation, leading to CO₂ washout.
    • Since CO₂ is the primary respiratory drive, its excessive removal leads to apnea.
    • As CO₂ builds up again, respiration resumes, creating the characteristic pattern.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apnea:

 

  • Apnea refers to a complete cessation of breathing without a preceding crescendo-decrescendo pattern.
  • CSR includes periodic breathing, not just apnea.

 

Option B. Biot’s Breathing:

 

  • Biot’s breathing is characterized by irregular, unpatterned breathing with sudden apneic episodes.
  • Seen in brainstem damage (e.g., bulbar polio, uremia).
  • Unlike CSR, Biot’s breathing does not follow a crescendo-decrescendo pattern.

 

Option D. Hyperpnea:

 

  • Hyperpnea is simply an increased rate and depth of breathing.
  • CSR consists of alternating phases of hyperpnea and apnea, whereas isolated hyperpnea does not include apnea.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern followed by apnea, seen in conditions like heart failure, high altitude, and brain injuries. It is caused by delayed feedback of CO₂ regulation in the respiratory centers.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about myocardium except:

options.label: A
options.text: Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and negative lusitropic effect

options.label: B
options.text: Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and positive lusitropic effect

options.label: C
options.text: Lusitropic effect is mediated by cAMP dependent pathway

options.label: D
options.text: Increase Ca2+ uptake from ECF to cytoplasm decreases lucitropy in the absence of sympathetic stimulation

questions.answerText: Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and negative lusitropic effect
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and negative lusitropic effect

 

Sympathetic activation affects both contraction (inotropic effect) and relaxation (lusitropic effect) in the myocardium.

 

  1. Positive Inotropic Effect (Increased Force of Contraction):
    • β1-adrenergic receptor activation → Increased cAMP → PKA activation
    • Leads to increased Ca²⁺ influx through L-type calcium channels, resulting in stronger myocardial contraction.
  2. Positive Lusitropic Effect (Faster Relaxation):
    • Phospholamban normally inhibits the SERCA pump (Sarcoplasmic/Endoplasmic Reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase), which reuptakes calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum for muscle relaxation.
    • Sympathetic stimulation phosphorylates phospholamban, removing its inhibition on the SERCA pump, allowing faster Ca²⁺ reuptake, which enhances relaxation.

 

Since sympathetic activity increases both inotropic and lusitropic effects, option A (which states a negative lusitropic effect) is incorrect. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Increase Sympathetic activity causes positive ionotropic and positive lusitropic effect: Sympathetic activation enhances both contraction (inotropic effect) and relaxation (lusitropic effect) via cAMP and PKA pathways.

 

Option C. Lusitropic effect is mediated by cAMP-dependent pathway: cAMP activates PKA, which phosphorylates phospholamban, leading to enhanced SERCA activity and faster relaxation.

 

Option D. Increase Ca²⁺ uptake from ECF to cytoplasm decreases lusitropy in the absence of sympathetic stimulation: If more Ca²⁺ enters the cytoplasm from the extracellular fluid without sympathetic stimulation, the Ca²⁺ remains high in the cytoplasm, delaying relaxation and reducing lusitropic effect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sympathetic stimulation enhances both inotropic (force of contraction) and lusitropic (relaxation) effects in the myocardium via β1-receptors, cAMP, and PKA-mediated phosphorylation of phospholamban, leading to increased SERCA activity.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with hematemesis has heart- burn and stomach pain. An endoscopy shows inflammation involving the gastric body and antrum as well as a small gastric ulcer. Biopsies were positive for H. pylori. H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa primarily by increasing mucosal levels of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ammonium

 

Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a gram-negative, urease-producing bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa, leading to gastritis, peptic ulcers, and even gastric cancer.

 

How does H. pylori damage the gastric mucosa?

 

  1. Urease Enzyme → Ammonium Production
    • H. pylori contains urease, which breaks down urea into ammonia (NH₃) and carbon dioxide (CO₂).
    • The ammonia neutralizes gastric acid, allowing the bacteria to survive in the acidic environment.
    • However, ammonia is toxic to epithelial cells and disrupts mucosal integrity.
  2. Increased Gastric Acid Secretion
    • The local buffering by ammonia fools the gastric epithelial cells into sensing a higher pH, leading to increased gastrin release and more HCl secretion.
    • This contributes to gastric mucosal damage and ulcer formation.
  3. Mucinase & Cytotoxins
    • Mucinase enzyme degrades the protective mucus layer, exposing gastric cells to acid and pepsin, further exacerbating tissue damage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bile Salts:

 

  • Bile salts are involved in fat digestion and absorption, but do not play a role in H. pylori-induced gastric damage.
  • Bile reflux gastritis is different from H. pylori gastritis.

 

Option C. Gastrin:

 

  • H. pylori increases gastric acid secretion, but not by directly increasing gastrin levels.
  • The increase in ammonium buffers acid, leading to a false sense of alkalinity, which then stimulates gastrin release indirectly.

 

Option D. NSAIDs:

 

  • NSAIDs cause gastric damage by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, leading to reduced mucus and bicarbonate production.
  • H. pylori does not increase NSAIDs, but both are major causes of peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

 

Educational Objective:

 

H. pylori damages the gastric mucosa primarily by producing urease, which breaks down urea into ammonium, increasing mucosal pH and leading to excessive acid secretion, mucosal injury, and ulcer formation.

questions.stem: All of the following are True in SIADH except:

options.label: B
options.text: Urine Na+ concentration < 20 mmol/L with normal salt intake

questions.answerText: Urine Na+ concentration < 20 mmol/L with normal salt intake
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Urine Na+ concentration < 20 mmol/L with normal salt intake

 

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excessive ADH release, leading to water retention, dilutional hyponatremia, and concentrated urine.

 

  1. Key Features of SIADH:
    • Increased ADH → Excessive water reabsorption → Dilution of plasma
    • Plasma osmolality ↓ (hypoosmolar serum)
    • Urine osmolality ↑ (concentrated urine)
    • Increased natriuresis due to Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) to maintain euvolemia
    • SIADH leads to increased urinary sodium excretion (> 20 mmol/L) despite normal salt intake due to ANP-mediated natriuresis.
    • The body compensates for excess water retention by excreting sodium in urine to maintain euvolemia.
    • Thus, urinary sodium concentration is NOT low (<20 mmol/L); rather, it is elevated (>20 mmol/L).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clinically Euvolemic & sometimes Hypervolemic:

 

  • Patients with SIADH are typically euvolemic, but mild hypervolemia can occur initially.
  • However, excess water is counteracted by ANP-mediated sodium excretion, leading to apparent euvolemia.

 

Option C. Serum Osmolarity < 275 mOsm/L:

 

  • SIADH causes water retention, leading to plasma dilution and reduced serum osmolarity (<275 mOsm/L).

 

Option D. Urine Osmolarity > 100 mOsm/L:

 

  • ADH increases water reabsorption, leading to concentrated urine with an osmolarity > 100 mOsm/L.
  • Normally, urine should be dilute in the presence of hyponatremia, but in SIADH, urine remains inappropriately concentrated.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SIADH is characterized by low plasma osmolality (<275 mOsm/L), high urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/L), and increased natriuresis (>20 mmol/L) despite normal salt intake due to ANP-mediated sodium excretion.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is suffering from common cold visited the hospital with complain of vomiting since three days and extreme weakness. Her examination and lab findings are as: BP - 90/60mmHg Pulse - 110/ min RR - 10 /min Blood pH - 7.6 Plasma bicarbonate - 30mEq/L, PCO2 - 45mmHg What should be patient’s current acid -base status and hormone involved:

options.label: B
options.text: Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II

options.label: C
options.text: Respiratory acidosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II

questions.answerText: Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II

 

This 32-year-old woman has been vomiting for three days, which is a key cause of metabolic alkalosis due to the loss of gastric acid (HCl).

 

  1. Step-by-step acid-base analysis:
    • pH = 7.6 → Alkalosis (Normal: 7.35–7.45)
    • Plasma Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) = 30 mEq/L (↑) → Metabolic Alkalosis (Normal: 22–28 mEq/L)
    • PCO₂ = 45 mmHg (↑)
      • The lungs are compensating by hypoventilation, leading to CO₂ retention (which is acidic).
      • This is a typical compensatory response to metabolic alkalosis.
  2. Hormonal Involvement:
    • Vomiting → Loss of HCl → Decreased extracellular fluid (ECF) volume → Hypovolemia → Activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
    • Aldosterone: Increases Na⁺ reabsorption, K⁺ excretion, and H⁺ excretion, worsening metabolic alkalosis.
    • Angiotensin II: Stimulates aldosterone release, causes vasoconstriction, and promotes sodium and water retention to restore blood pressure.
  3. Why not ANP?
    • Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) is released in response to hypervolemia (high blood volume), not hypovolemia.
    • Since the patient has low BP (90/60 mmHg), ANP is NOT activated. Instead, RAAS is activated.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metabolic alkalosis, aldosterone and ANP:

 

  • ANP is NOT involved in this condition because the patient is hypovolemic, and ANP promotes natriuresis, which would worsen the hypovolemia.

 

Option C. Respiratory acidosis, aldosterone and angiotensin II:

 

  • The pH is elevated (7.6), NOT decreased, ruling out acidosis.
  • The primary cause of the disturbance is metabolic (high bicarbonate), not respiratory.

 

Option D. Respiratory acidosis, aldosterone and ANP:

 

  • The patient has metabolic alkalosis, not respiratory acidosis.
  • ANP is not activated in hypovolemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Prolonged vomiting leads to metabolic alkalosis due to the loss of HCl, which triggers hypovolemia and activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), leading to sodium and water retention. ANP is not activated in hypovolemia.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital after experiencing nausea and vomiting for about 2 days followed by severe muscle weakness and neurological symptoms including ptosis and dysphagia. She told the resident doctor on duty that she had dinner in a restaurant the evening before the symptoms began. Her lab tests were positive for Clostridium botulinum. What could be the basis of muscle weakness in this case?

options.label: A
options.text: Blocked the reuptake of neurotransmitter into the presynaptic nerve terminal.

options.label: B
options.text: Bound irreversibly to the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

options.label: C
options.text: Prevented the release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal.

options.label: D
options.text: Exerted its adverse effects by a direct action on the skeletal muscle.

questions.answerText: Prevented the release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Prevented the release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal

 

The patient is suffering from botulism, a condition caused by Clostridium botulinum toxin. This toxin specifically inhibits the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by blocking the function of SNARE proteins like synaptobrevin, which are necessary for the exocytosis of acetylcholine. Without acetylcholine release, the muscles are unable to contract, leading to symptoms like muscle weakness, ptosis, and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). This flaccid paralysis is characteristic of botulism and highlights the role of the toxin in preventing acetylcholine release, thus affecting muscle function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blocked the reuptake of neurotransmitter into the presynaptic nerve terminal: This option is incorrect because botulinum toxin does not interfere with the reuptake of neurotransmitters. Instead, it acts by blocking the release of acetylcholine, which prevents nerve impulses from triggering muscle contractions.

 

Option B. Bound irreversibly to the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane: This is incorrect because botulinum toxin does not bind to postsynaptic receptors. Instead, it inhibits the release of acetylcholine before it reaches the postsynaptic membrane.

 

Option D. Exerted its adverse effects by a direct action on the skeletal muscle: This is incorrect as the toxin does not directly affect muscle tissue. The toxin’s primary action occurs at the nerve terminal, where it prevents acetylcholine release, indirectly leading to muscle weakness.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Botulinum toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by inhibiting SNARE proteins, leading to muscle weakness and flaccid paralysis.

questions.stem: Assume that excess blood is transfused into a patient whose arterial baroreceptors are non-functional and whose blood pressure increases from 100 to 150 mm Hg. Then, assume that the same volume of blood is infused into the same patient under conditions in which his arterial baroreceptors are functioning normally, and blood pressure increases from 100 to 125 mm Hg. What is the approximate feedback "gain" of the arterial baroreceptors in this patient when they are functioning normally?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) -1.0

 

Feedback gain is a measure of how well a regulatory system, such as the baroreceptor system, corrects a disturbance. The gain is calculated as the ratio of the correction to the error. In this case, we need to calculate how well the baroreceptors corrected the increase in blood pressure after the blood infusion.

 

  1. Without baroreceptor function, blood pressure increased from 100 to 150 mm Hg, a 50 mm Hg increase.
  2. With baroreceptor function, blood pressure increased from 100 to 125 mm Hg, a 25 mm Hg increase.

 

The correction is the difference between the increase without baroreceptors (50 mm Hg) and the increase with baroreceptors (25 mm Hg), so the correction is 25 mm Hg.

 

The error is the difference between the final blood pressure with baroreceptors (125 mm Hg) and the original blood pressure (100 mm Hg), which is 25 mm Hg.

The negative sign indicates that this is a negative feedback system, where the correction opposes the initial disturbance.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The gain of the baroreceptor system is calculated as the ratio of correction to error. In a negative feedback system like the baroreceptor reflex, this gain is typically negative, indicating opposition to the original disturbance. In this case, the gain is -1.0.

questions.stemHtml: Preload is the stretching of the cardiac muscle fibers at the end of diastole, just before contraction. It is due to an increase in ventricular pressure caused by the filling of blood during diastole. An image is provided that further supplements the findings stated above. These are expressions of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Frank-Starling’s law

 

The Frank-Starling law explains the relationship between ventricular preload (end-diastolic volume or EDV) and stroke volume. According to this law, within physiological limits, an increase in preload (the initial stretching of the cardiac muscle fibers due to increased blood volume) results in an increase in stroke volume. This is because the increased stretching of the fibers enhances the force of contraction by increasing the sensitivity of troponin C and facilitating better actin-myosin cross-bridge formation.

 

The provided diagram shows the ventricular preload on the x-axis and stroke volume on the y-axis, illustrating that, as preload increases (in the preload-dependent zone), stroke volume also increases, which is exactly what Frank-Starling's law predicts. In the preload-independent zone, stroke volume plateaus, indicating that beyond a certain preload, further increases do not enhance stroke volume.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vascular hyalinosis: This refers to the pathological deposition of hyaline material in blood vessels, commonly associated with conditions such as hypertension or diabetes. It is not related to the preload-stroke volume relationship in cardiac function.

 

Option C. Vascular capacitance: Vascular capacitance is the ability of blood vessels, particularly veins, to store blood. While this concept relates to venous return, it does not directly describe the relationship between preload and stroke volume as described by the Frank-Starling mechanism.

 

Option D. Vascular resistance: Vascular resistance refers to the opposition to blood flow within the vessels, primarily in the arterioles. It affects blood pressure and flow but does not explain the preload-stroke volume relationship in the heart.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Frank-Starling’s law explains that increased preload (end-diastolic volume) leads to increased stroke volume due to enhanced muscle fiber stretching and increased force of contraction within physiological limits.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with complaints of right-sided weakness and jargon speech. A CT brain was ordered to rule out hemorrhagic stroke. On neurological examination, there is normal object recognition but loss of comprehension. Which of the following areas is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior temporal gyrus

 

The superior temporal gyrus contains Wernicke's area, which is responsible for language comprehension. In this case, the patient presents with fluent but nonsensical speech (jargon speech) and loss of comprehension, both of which are classic symptoms of Wernicke's aphasia. Wernicke's aphasia occurs when the Wernicke's area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, is damaged. Patients with this condition can speak fluently, but their speech lacks meaning, and they are unable to comprehend spoken language, despite normal object recognition.

 

This patient's right-sided weakness suggests a left-sided brain lesion, as language centers like Wernicke's area are typically located in the left hemisphere for right-handed individuals. The jargon speech and loss of comprehension directly point to the superior temporal gyrus as the affected area.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior frontal gyrus: This area contains Broca's area, responsible for speech production. Damage to Broca’s area results in non-fluent speech and difficulty forming words (Broca's aphasia). However, comprehension remains intact, which is not the case in this scenario.

 

Option C. Arcuate fasciculus: The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke’s area to Broca’s area and is involved in the repetition of speech. Damage to this area causes conduction aphasia, characterized by intact comprehension and fluent speech but impaired ability to repeat words. In this case, comprehension is affected, so this is not the correct answer.

 

Option D. Both A & B: While both Wernicke's (superior temporal gyrus) and Broca's (inferior frontal gyrus) areas are important for language, only the superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke’s area) is relevant in this patient, as the main issue is with comprehension, not speech production.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Damage to the superior temporal gyrus, particularly Wernicke’s area, results in fluent but nonsensical speech (jargon speech) and loss of comprehension, typical of Wernicke's aphasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are incorrect about vasopressin?

options.label: A
options.text: It's a more powerful vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II.

options.label: B
options.text: Concentration of circulating blood vasopressin after severe hemorrhage can increase enough to attenuate reductions in arterial pressure markedly.

options.label: C
options.text: Uses adenylyl cyclase-cAMP as well as phospholipase C system.

options.label: D
options.text: Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus

questions.answerText: Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Secreted by paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus

 

Vasopressin, also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH), is primarily secreted by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus, not the paraventricular nucleus. The paraventricular nucleus is mainly involved in the secretion of oxytocin. Therefore, statement D is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It's a more powerful vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II: This is correct. Vasopressin (ADH) is indeed a more potent vasoconstrictor than angiotensin II, as it acts on all blood vessels, whereas angiotensin II primarily acts on the afferent and efferent arterioles of the kidneys.

 

Option B. Concentration of circulating blood vasopressin after severe hemorrhage can increase enough to attenuate reductions in arterial pressure markedly: This is correct. During severe hemorrhage, vasopressin levels in the blood can rise significantly, helping to maintain blood pressure by reducing the extent of the drop in arterial pressure.

 

Option C. Uses adenylyl cyclase-cAMP as well as phospholipase C system: This is correct. Vasopressin works through different signaling pathways depending on the receptor subtype. Through the V2 receptor, it activates the adenylyl cyclase-cAMP pathway, and through the V1 receptor, it acts via the phospholipase C system (IP3-DAG pathway).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vasopressin (ADH) is secreted by the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus, not the paraventricular nucleus. It is a potent vasoconstrictor and plays a crucial role in maintaining blood pressure during states of volume depletion such as hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old smoker having difficulty in breathing was diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and has an oxygen saturation of 89%. The cause of this reduced saturation is a defect in which mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Simple diffusion

 

Pulmonary fibrosis leads to thickening of the alveolar walls, which impairs the simple diffusion of gases, including oxygen, across the alveolar-capillary membrane. Oxygen moves from the alveoli to the blood via simple diffusion, driven by the partial pressure gradient. In conditions like pulmonary fibrosis, the increased thickness of the alveolar walls slows down the diffusion of oxygen, leading to reduced oxygen saturation levels, as seen in this patient (89%).

 

Simple diffusion is the passive movement of gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide through the alveolar membrane, and it does not require transporters or energy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Facilitated diffusion: Facilitated diffusion involves the use of carrier proteins to move substances across cell membranes. However, gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide do not require carriers; they diffuse directly through membranes, so this mechanism is not involved in gas exchange in the lungs.

 

Option C. Primary active transport: Primary active transport requires energy (ATP) to move substances against a concentration gradient. Since gas exchange in the lungs is a passive process, this option is incorrect.

 

Option D. Secondary active transport: This mechanism also requires energy and involves the movement of molecules coupled with the movement of another substance, typically ions. Again, this does not apply to gas exchange in the lungs.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The diffusion of gases, such as oxygen and carbon dioxide, across the alveolar membrane occurs via simple diffusion, which is impaired in conditions like pulmonary fibrosis, leading to reduced oxygen saturation.

questions.stemHtml: True statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve is?

options.label: B
options.text: At point E, the nerve is more excitable

options.label: C
options.text: Point C to D is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels

options.label: D
options.text: Point B to D is refractory period

questions.answerText: Point B to D is refractory period
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Point B to D is refractory period

 

The refractory period is the time during which the nerve cannot generate another action potential, regardless of the strength of the stimulus. Point B to D on the curve represents this period. During this phase, sodium (Na+) channels are either still open or inactivated, and potassium (K+) channels begin to open, which contributes to the cell repolarizing. Specifically, this phase is referred to as the absolute refractory period because no additional action potential can be triggered, regardless of the stimulus strength.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Threshold point is at A: Incorrect. Point A represents the resting membrane potential (RMP), not the threshold. The threshold is the membrane potential that must be reached for an action potential to be triggered, typically occurring between point A and B.

 

Option B. At point E, the nerve is more excitable: Incorrect. Point E represents hyperpolarization, where the membrane potential is more negative than the resting potential. This makes the nerve less excitable, as it would require a stronger stimulus to bring the membrane potential back to the threshold.

 

Option C. Point C to D is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels: Incorrect. Point C to D represents the repolarization phase, which is primarily due to the opening of potassium (K+) channels and the inactivation of sodium (Na+) channels, leading to the membrane potential becoming more negative.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The refractory period is the time between points B and D on the action potential curve, where the neuron is unable to fire another action potential. This period is critical for ensuring that action potentials only travel in one direction along the neuron.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of transport across the cell membrane represented below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Facilitated diffusion

 

The image shows carrier proteins embedded in the cell membrane facilitating the movement of molecules from the extracellular space to the intracellular space. The key feature of facilitated diffusion is that it utilizes specific carrier proteins to help transport substances down their concentration gradient (from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration), without the use of energy (ATP).

 

In this case, the green molecules in the extracellular space are moving along the gradient with the help of the carrier proteins, which undergo conformational changes to allow the passage of these molecules.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Simple diffusion: Simple diffusion involves the passive movement of molecules directly through the lipid bilayer without the aid of carrier proteins. Since the image clearly shows carrier proteins assisting the movement, simple diffusion is not the correct mechanism.

 

Option C. Primary active transport: This involves the movement of substances against their concentration gradient with the use of energy (ATP). The image does not depict energy usage, and the movement is along the gradient, so this is incorrect.

 

Option D. Secondary active transport: Secondary active transport involves the movement of one substance down its gradient to drive the movement of another substance against its gradient. The image shows only passive movement along the concentration gradient, so this option is also incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Facilitated diffusion allows molecules to move down their concentration gradient with the help of carrier proteins, without the use of energy, which is the mechanism shown in the image.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A preterm baby who was delivered at 28 weeks developed respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is true about surface tension and compliance in this baby?

options.label: C
options.text: Both surface tension and compliance decreased

options.label: D
options.text: Both surface tension and compliance increased

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Surface tension - increased; Compliance - decreased

 

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm infants is often caused by a deficiency in surfactant production. Surfactant, a substance produced by the lungs, helps reduce surface tension at the air-water interface within the alveoli, preventing collapse during exhalation and increasing lung compliance (the ability of the lungs to expand).

 

In preterm babies, especially those born before 34 weeks of gestation, there is insufficient production of surfactant. This leads to an increase in surface tension, as the alveoli have difficulty remaining open due to the lack of surfactant to counteract the inward force. With increased surface tension, the lungs become less compliant, meaning the lungs are stiffer and require more effort to expand.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Surface tension - decreased; Compliance - increased: This is incorrect because surfactant deficiency leads to increased surface tension, not decreased, and compliance is reduced, not increased, in respiratory distress syndrome.

 

Option C. Both surface tension and compliance decreased: This is incorrect because surface tension increases in the absence of sufficient surfactant, and as a result, lung compliance decreases.

 

Option D. Both surface tension and compliance increased: This is incorrect because increased surface tension is associated with decreased compliance, as seen in respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In preterm babies with respiratory distress syndrome, surface tension increases due to a lack of surfactant, and lung compliance decreases, making it harder for the lungs to expand.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect with respect to Resting Membrane Potential in different cell types?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Smooth muscle: −8 to −12 mV

 

The resting membrane potential (RMP) of smooth muscle cells is typically around −50 to −60 mV, not −8 to −12 mV. The incorrect range given in option D (−8 to −12 mV) is closer to the RMP of red blood cells (RBCs), which have the lowest resting membrane potential due to their limited excitability.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Neurons: −60 to −70 mV: This is correct. The resting membrane potential of neurons typically ranges from −60 to −70 mV. This allows neurons to quickly depolarize and fire action potentials when stimulated.

 

Option B. Skeletal muscle: −85 to −95 mV: This is correct. Skeletal muscle cells have a more negative resting membrane potential compared to neurons, typically between −85 and −95 mV, which helps maintain stability before contraction.

 

Option C. Hair (cochlea): −15 to −40 mV: This is correct. Hair cells in the cochlea have a unique RMP that can range from −15 to −40 mV depending on the ionic conditions, particularly the potassium levels in the endolymph.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The resting membrane potential of smooth muscle cells is around −50 to −60 mV, and the incorrect range provided in the question (−8 to −12 mV) is more characteristic of red blood cells (RBCs).

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Arrange the following steps of ventricular action potential in the correct order: Opening of voltage-gated calcium channelsRepolarizing K+ currentsOpening of voltage-gated sodium channelsTransient outward flow of potassium
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C, D, A, B

 

The ventricular action potential progresses through specific stages, primarily driven by the flow of sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), and calcium (Ca2+) ions through their respective channels. The correct sequence is:

 

  1. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (C): The action potential begins with a rapid depolarization caused by the opening of sodium channels, allowing Na+ ions to rush into the cell. This depolarizes the membrane and brings the membrane potential to a positive value.
  2. Transient outward flow of potassium (D): After the initial depolarization, there is a brief phase of partial repolarization due to a transient outward flow of potassium ions (Ito current), which begins to bring the membrane potential back down slightly.
  3. Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels (A): This leads to the plateau phase, where calcium ions enter the cell through voltage-gated calcium channels. During this phase, the membrane potential remains relatively stable because Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux are balanced.
  4. Repolarizing K+ currents (B): Finally, repolarization occurs as voltage-gated potassium channels open more fully, allowing potassium to leave the cell, bringing the membrane potential back to its resting state.

 

Thus, the correct sequence is C → D → A → B.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sequence of events in the ventricular action potential begins with sodium influx, followed by transient potassium outflow, calcium influx during the plateau, and finally potassium efflux for repolarization.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: A 40-year-old male diagnosed with bronchial asthma for the past 10 years underwent pulmonary function tests to assess lung function. Which of the following is true?

options.label: B
options.text: VC reduces but FEV1 is normal

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) VC normal but FEV1 reduces

 

Bronchial asthma is an obstructive lung disease (OLD), where the main issue lies in airway obstruction, leading to difficulty in exhaling air. In such cases, FEV1 (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second) is reduced because of the narrowed airways that make it difficult to expel air quickly. However, Vital Capacity (VC), which represents the total volume of air a person can exhale after a full inhalation, remains normal because the lungs can still take in air, but the expulsion is slower due to obstruction.

  • In asthma (an obstructive condition), FEV1 decreases while VC (or FVC) is typically unaffected, leading to a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, which is characteristic of obstructive lung disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. VC reduces but FEV1 is normal: This pattern is more characteristic of restrictive lung disease (RLD), where the lungs' ability to expand is compromised, reducing total lung volumes, including VC. In asthma (OLD), VC remains normal while FEV1 is reduced.

 

Option C. FEV1/FVC ratio normal: In obstructive lung diseases like asthma, the FEV1/FVC ratio is decreased due to a greater reduction in FEV1 compared to FVC, not normal.

 

Option D. Functional residual capacity reduces: In obstructive lung disease, functional residual capacity (FRC), which is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after normal exhalation, is often increased, not reduced, due to air trapping from the airway obstruction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In obstructive lung diseases such as asthma, the FEV1 decreases due to airway obstruction, but vital capacity (VC) remains normal.

questions.stem: Which of the following jugular venous pressure (JVP) waves corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C wave

 

The C wave in the jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle. This phase occurs when the ventricles begin to contract but there is no ejection of blood yet because both the aortic and pulmonary valves are still closed. During this phase, the tricuspid valve bulges into the right atrium, causing a brief rise in atrial pressure, which is reflected as the C wave in the JVP.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A wave: This wave represents atrial contraction (the last phase of diastole), which occurs just before ventricular contraction. It does not correspond to the isovolumetric contraction phase.

 

Option C. X descent: The X descent represents atrial relaxation and the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve during ventricular systole, but it does not correspond directly to the isovolumetric contraction phase.

 

Option D. Y descent: The Y descent represents the rapid emptying of the atrium into the ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens. It is part of diastole and does not correspond to isovolumetric contraction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The C wave in the jugular venous pressure waveform corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle, marked by the tricuspid valve bulging into the right atrium.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the segment with the bolus of food during peristalsis is because of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) VIP

 

During peristalsis, as a bolus of food moves through the intestine, there is a coordinated contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle segments. The segment behind the bolus contracts to push the bolus forward, while the segment ahead of the bolus must relax to allow the bolus to move along the intestinal tract.

 

The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the bolus is primarily mediated by VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide) and Nitric Oxide (NO). These substances act as neurotransmitters, released by inhibitory neurons in the enteric nervous system, causing smooth muscle relaxation in the area ahead of the bolus. This relaxation allows the bolus to move smoothly through the intestines in the direction from mouth to anus, known as the cranial-portal direction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Substance P: Substance P is involved in the contraction of smooth muscle, specifically in the segment behind the bolus of food, not relaxation of the distal segment.

 

Option C. Dopamine from adrenergic fibers: Dopamine does not play a primary role in the relaxation of smooth muscle during peristalsis. VIP and NO are the main mediators.

 

Option D. Acetylcholine from myenteric fibers: Acetylcholine is primarily involved in smooth muscle contraction, especially in the segment behind the bolus, not relaxation of the distal segment.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The relaxation of the intestinal segment distal to the bolus during peristalsis is mediated by VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide) and Nitric Oxide, allowing smooth movement of the bolus along the intestine.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: All of the following increase gastric acid secretion except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Serotonin

 

Gastric acid secretion is regulated by several factors, including gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine, which stimulate the parietal cells in the stomach to release hydrochloric acid (HCl). These three agents work synergistically to increase gastric acid production.

 

Serotonin (5-HT) plays various roles in the gastrointestinal system, but it does not stimulate gastric acid secretion. Instead, serotonin is more involved in regulating gut motility and promoting smooth muscle contractions.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gastrin: Secreted by G-cells, gastrin stimulates the parietal cells directly and indirectly (via histamine release) to increase acid secretion.

 

Option B. Histamine: Released by enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, histamine binds to H2 receptors on parietal cells and strongly stimulates acid production.

 

Option C. Acetylcholine: Released by the vagus nerve, acetylcholine stimulates parietal cells via muscarinic receptors to secrete gastric acid.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Serotonin does not increase gastric acid secretion, whereas gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine are major stimulators of acid production in the stomach.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: The stroke volume depends on end-diastolic volume. This is best represented as?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Length-tension relationship

 

The relationship between stroke volume and end-diastolic volume (EDV) is best represented by the length-tension relationship, which is a key component of Frank-Starling’s law of the heart. According to this law, the force of contraction in cardiac muscle is proportional to the initial length of the muscle fibers (end-diastolic volume). As the ventricles fill with more blood (increasing EDV), the myocardial fibers stretch, increasing their length. This, in turn, enhances the tension generated during contraction, leading to a greater stroke volume.

 

Thus, the length-tension relationship describes how the initial stretching of the cardiac muscle (related to EDV) affects the tension generated (which influences stroke volume).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Length-force relationship: This term could be confused with the length-tension relationship, but it does not specifically refer to the role of muscle stretch and tension as seen in cardiac physiology.

 

Option B. Length-velocity relationship: This describes how muscle shortening velocity decreases as load increases, which is not directly related to stroke volume or EDV.

 

Option D. Length-viscosity relationship: This term does not apply to the mechanical properties of cardiac muscle contraction and stroke volume.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The length-tension relationship explains how the stroke volume of the heart is affected by the end-diastolic volume (EDV), as described by Frank-Starling’s law.

questions.stem: A team of climbers is being briefed about the physiological changes that occur in the body at high altitudes. Which of the following is not a typical physiological response seen in individuals at high altitudes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypoventilation

 

At high altitudes, the body undergoes several physiological adaptations to cope with decreased oxygen availability (hypoxia). Hypoventilation (incorrect): Hypoventilation does not occur at high altitudes. Instead, hyperventilation occurs as a response to hypoxia. The body increases the rate and depth of breathing (hyperventilation) to compensate for low oxygen levels in the environment. This helps increase oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide elimination.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Polycythemia: This is a compensatory increase in red blood cell (RBC) production, driven by increased erythropoietin release, which enhances oxygen-carrying capacity. Polycythemia helps deliver more oxygen to tissues.

 

Option B. Increase in Hemoglobin (Hb) concentration: To improve oxygen transport in a hypoxic environment, the body increases hemoglobin levels, allowing more oxygen to be carried in the blood.

 

Option C. Increase in Myoglobin: Myoglobin is a protein found in muscle tissue, including skeletal muscle and the heart, that binds oxygen with high affinity. At high altitudes, myoglobin increases, aiding in oxygen storage and utilization, particularly in muscles.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hypoventilation is not a typical response at high altitudes; instead, hyperventilation occurs to improve oxygen uptake in the hypoxic environment.

questions.stem: A patient experiences bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea following the administration of intravenous irritants during a medical procedure. These symptoms are suggestive of a specific reflex response. Which one of the following reflexes is most likely being represented in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Bezold-Jarisch reflex

 

The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is a cardiovascular reflex that leads to bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea in response to certain stimuli, such as intravenous irritants. This reflex is mediated through the vagus nerve, which is strongly activated in response to the irritants, leading to the classic triad of symptoms. It is characterized by an excessive vagal response that decreases heart rate (bradycardia), lowers blood pressure (hypotension), and causes a temporary cessation of breathing (apnea).

 

This reflex is typically triggered during medical procedures, especially when intravenous drugs or irritants are administered.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Bainbridge reflex: This reflex causes increased heart rate (tachycardia) in response to increased venous return (e.g., rapid infusion of fluids), leading to right atrial distension. This is the opposite of what is described in the scenario, which involves bradycardia.

 

Option C. Cushing’s reflex: Cushing’s reflex is a response to increased intracranial pressure (ICP). It typically presents as hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration. This reflex is not associated with intravenous irritants but with elevated intracranial pressure.

 

Option D. Valsalva maneuver: The Valsalva maneuver involves forceful expiration against a closed glottis, increasing intrathoracic pressure. This maneuver is used to assess autonomic function but does not cause the triad of bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea seen with the Bezold-Jarisch reflex.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is characterized by bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea, usually triggered by intravenous irritants or certain medical procedures, and is mediated through excessive vagal activation.

questions.stemHtml: In the presented spirometry image, what term corresponds to the point labeled as ‘F’ and ‘C’ respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: Expiratory reserve volume and Vital capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Vital capacity and Total lung capacity

options.label: C
options.text: Vital capacity and Expiratory reserve volume

options.label: D
options.text: Inspiratory capacity and Expiratory reserve volume

questions.answerText: Vital capacity and Expiratory reserve volume
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vital capacity and Expiratory reserve volume

 

In the provided spirometry graph:

  • F represents Vital Capacity (VC), which is the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation. It includes tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume.
  • C represents Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV), which is the additional air that can be exhaled after the normal tidal exhalation.

Thus, the correct answer is C. Vital capacity and Expiratory reserve volume.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Expiratory reserve volume and Vital capacity: This is incorrect because F represents vital capacity, not expiratory reserve volume, and C represents expiratory reserve volume.

 

Option B. Vital capacity and Total lung capacity: This is incorrect because F represents vital capacity, but C is not total lung capacity; it is expiratory reserve volume.

 

Option D. Inspiratory capacity and Expiratory reserve volume: This is incorrect because F represents vital capacity, not inspiratory capacity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In spirometry, Vital Capacity (F) is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a deep inhalation, and Expiratory Reserve Volume (C) is the volume of air that can be forcefully exhaled after a normal tidal exhalation.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: Kinesin, dynein and myosin proteins are an example of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Transport protein

 

Kinesin, dynein, and myosin are examples of transport proteins, also known as molecular motor proteins. These proteins are involved in intracellular transport, particularly in the movement of organelles, vesicles, and other cellular components along cytoskeletal tracks, such as microtubules and actin filaments.

  • Kinesin: Moves cargo in an anterograde direction, typically towards the plus end of microtubules, away from the nucleus.
  • Dynein: Moves cargo in a retrograde direction, towards the minus end of microtubules, toward the nucleus.
  • Myosin: Moves cargo along actin filaments and is also involved in muscle contraction.

These motor proteins play crucial roles in axoplasmic transport in neurons and other essential intracellular processes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cell membrane protein: Incorrect, as kinesin, dynein, and myosin are not proteins found in the cell membrane; they are cytoplasmic transport proteins.

 

Option B. Cell organelle adherent protein: Incorrect, adherent proteins like cadherins and catenins help bind cells together but are not involved in transport like kinesin, dynein, or myosin.

 

Option C. Intercellular junctional protein: Incorrect, intercellular junctional proteins facilitate cell-to-cell adhesion, such as in tight junctions or desmosomes, not intracellular transport.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Kinesin, dynein and myosin are transport proteins that move cargo along cytoskeletal structures within the cell, playing key roles in intracellular transport and processes like axoplasmic transport in neurons.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 035-Anat, Physio & Biochem Test (The Champion Batch Hyderabad) - 15-09-2025 - 2025-09-15
questions.stem: In a patient with a known bleeding disorder, dysfunction of which cellular organelle responsible for intracellular packaging could potentially result in impaired secretion of clotting factors and other crucial proteins?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Golgi Apparatus

 

The Golgi Apparatus is the organelle responsible for the intracellular packaging of proteins, including clotting factors. After proteins are synthesized in the ribosome and transported through the endoplasmic reticulum, they are delivered to the Golgi Apparatus. Here, they are processed, modified, sorted, and packaged into vesicles for secretion or transport to their appropriate destination. In the case of clotting factors, dysfunction in the Golgi Apparatus would lead to improper packaging and secretion, potentially resulting in a bleeding disorder due to inadequate clotting proteins being released into circulation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Ribosome: Ribosomes are responsible for the synthesis of proteins, not their packaging. While they play a crucial role in protein production, they are not involved in the intracellular transport or secretion of proteins, which is necessary for clotting factors.

 

Option C. Cytoplasm: The cytoplasm is the fluid matrix inside the cell where many biochemical reactions occur, but it is not involved in packaging or secretion of proteins. It serves more as the location where organelles like the Golgi Apparatus and ribosomes are found.

 

Option D. Lysosome: Lysosomes are primarily involved in the breakdown and recycling of cellular waste and macromolecules. They are not involved in the packaging or secretion of proteins and therefore would not affect clotting factor secretion.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The Golgi Apparatus is responsible for the intracellular packaging and secretion of proteins, including clotting factors. Dysfunction of this organelle can lead to impaired secretion, potentially contributing to bleeding disorders.

questions.stem: Which one of the following membranes has the highest content of protein per gram of tissue?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Inner mitochondrial membrane

 

The inner mitochondrial membrane has the highest content of proteins per gram of tissue. This membrane is packed with proteins because it contains the electron transport chain and ATP synthase complexes, which are essential for cellular respiration and energy production. These proteins are critical for oxidative phosphorylation, the process that generates ATP, the cell's energy currency. The high demand for energy in cells explains the abundance of protein in this membrane.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Outer mitochondrial membrane: The outer mitochondrial membrane has a balanced lipid-to-protein ratio of 1:1, meaning it does not have as high a concentration of proteins as the inner mitochondrial membrane.

 

Option B. Myelin sheath: The myelin sheath is rich in lipids rather than proteins. It primarily serves as insulation for nerve fibers, facilitating rapid transmission of electrical impulses. Therefore, the lipid content is much higher than the protein content.

 

Option D. Plasma membrane: The plasma membrane, like the outer mitochondrial membrane, has a lipid-to-protein ratio of about 1:1. It functions as a selective barrier around the cell, with proteins embedded within it, but it does not have as high a protein concentration as the inner mitochondrial membrane.

 

Educational Objective :

 

The inner mitochondrial membrane has the highest protein content among the listed membranes, reflecting its crucial role in energy production and cellular respiration.
